title: Victoria Point woman waited seven hours for ambulance before death
text:
The ABC understands a woman who died in Brisbane last month was left waiting almost seven hours for an ambulance.

The 63-year-old woman died at Victoria Point after repeated calls for an ambulance.

At least six Queenslanders have died in recent weeks, with some people waiting as long as 18 hours for an ambulance.

Queensland health minister Tim Nicholls said last week the government was pulling "every possible lever" to deliver more hospital beds, while also calling on the Commonwealth to provide more aged care beds.

Premier David Crisafulli has said the health system's issues could be resolved "overnight" with more federal funding.

Federal frontbencher Murray Watt has pushed back against calls for more Commonwealth health funding. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

But federal frontbencher Murray Watt said the Queensland government needed to "take responsibility" for managing public health.

Minister Watt said state premiers had always "sought to blame Canberra for their woes".

"Running public hospitals and ambulance services is the responsibility of the state government and the state government needs to take responsibility for that here," he said.

" It's an absolute tragedy that we've seen Queenslanders lose their lives in recent times waiting for ambulances. The premier and his health minister need to step up and solve this. "

Opposition leader Steven Miles said: "Nobody deserves to die helpless and in agony".

"Sadly, that's what we've learned has been the end-of-life experience for seven Queenslanders over just the last few weeks," he said.

The Queensland Ambulance Service said the death of any patient is a tragedy and that it is providing support to the woman's family.

title: Roos survive Swans scare to book trip to fourth straight AFLW decider
text:
North Melbourne is within touching distance of an AFLW premiership "three-peat" after fighting out a 32-point victory over a Chloe Molloy-inspired Sydney in their preliminary final.

Ash Riddell and veteran Emma Kearney were centre stage as the Kangaroos kicked six goals clear in the first half before holding off a brave Swans challenge in the 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51) triumph at Princes Park on Saturday.

Darren Crocker's all-conquering side is into a fourth consecutive grand final, with the chance to complete the first flag hat-trick in the history of the women's competition.

North will take on the winner of Saturday's second preliminary final between Melbourne and Carlton.

But there is some concern over ruck Kim Rennie, who spent some time on the turf in the final quarter and eventually hobbled off with what appeared to be a right knee injury.

Riddell (29 disposals) and Eilish Sheerin (22) were outstanding, while superstar Jasmine Garner finished with three goals from 18 disposals despite attention from Swans tagger Tanya Kennedy.

Tahlia Randall and Blaithin Bogue kicked two each for the Kangaroos.

Kearney (15 disposals) was dependable as always on managed minutes in her return from a hamstring injury, and got under her opponents' skin in trademark fashion.

Molloy (three goals) did her best to lift Sydney, sparking a second-quarter fightback, but North had a greater number of contributors across the ground.

Laura Gardner (25 disposals), Zippy Fish (18) and Cynthia Hamilton (two goals) also fought hard for the gallant Swans.

A global Ticketmaster outage caused long queues for frustrated fans outside the ground, but those lucky enough to get in early witnessed a slice of history.

Hamilton opened the scoring for Sydney with the fastest AFLW goal, finishing well on the run just 21 seconds into the contest.

But Garner responded within a minute, and the opening term belonged to North, who led 4.2 to 2.1 at the first break.

Garner added her second early in the second quarter and it opened the floodgates, with the Kangaroos piling on another four consecutive goals.

Molloy breathed life back into the contest with three of Sydney's four goals in a nine-minute burst before half-time.

The Swans' superstar caught both Riddell and Kearney holding the ball, and kicked team-lifting goals against the tide.

The North duo demonstrably disputed the decisions with umpires but were not penalised further for dissent.

Kearney also sparked a melee when she riled her opponents by sarcastically joining in the Swans' celebrations.

Molloy's third major cut what was a 36-point margin back to 18 by half-time, with North leading 9.2 to 6.2 at the main break.

It was one goal apiece in a tight third quarter and the Swans got within a couple of kicks when Maddie Quinn (two goals) kicked the first major of the final term.

But North held firm and Garner kicked the sealer when she snapped her third major with less than four minutes left on the clock.

AAP

title: Spirit IV ferry docks late again after 'technical issue'
text:
One of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has once again docked hours behind schedule because of a "technical issue" with its primary navigational system.

Spirit IV was heading towards Geelong when the issue occurred early on Saturday morning, resulting in a tugboat being called to escort the vessel and passengers being dropped off four hours late.

A track map shows the ferry started to perform a series of loops within Port Phillip Bay from about 4.40am, with the vessel only resuming its course towards Geelong about 8am.

The Spirit of Tasmania IV spent more than three hours performing a series of loops early on Saturday morning. (Supplied: MarineTraffic)

TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone apologised for the inconvenience to passengers but said "safety is a more important consideration than meeting schedule".

"We experienced a minor technical issue with the primary navigational system, but at no point was Spirit of Tasmania IV at risk," Mr Carbone said.

"The secondary system performed as designed and the Master acted in accordance with his training."

The ABC understands the issue was related to the same steering fault that previously caused the Spirit IV to arrive four hours late into Geelong on November 5.

This is the second time the Spirit of Tasmania IV has been escorted into Geelong by a tugboat, following a similar incident in early November. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

One passenger posted on social media that the vessel was roughly on time before they were advised it "requires assistance from a tugboat", while another said it was "another day, another technical hitch" for Spirit IV.

Mr Carbone said the incident was "reported to the relevant authorities" and there was not expected to be any delay to the departure time for the Spirit IV's journey from Geelong to Devonport on Saturday night.

As a result of the incident in early November, TT-Line announced it had suspended the use of autopilot on the new vessels within Port Phillip Bay while it probed the steering faults.

That incident is being investigated by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, which is also looking into a separate steering fault which affected the Spirit V on a trial voyage in October.

The two vessels started ferrying passengers between Devonport and Geelong last month when they replaced the Spirit of Tasmania I and II.

title: Honda, Toyota recall 1.6 million US vehicles over airbag rupture risk
text:
Car makers Honda and Toyota have announced they are recalling about 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs in the US over a risk that their Takata airbag inflators could rupture.

Honda and Toyota both said there were no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no airbag inflator ruptures.

But the companies added that they would replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles.

There have been at least 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009, an issue prompting the largest recall in US motoring history.

All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a drying agent, with at least 20 of those fatalities occurring in Honda vehicles.

More than 20 car companies have recalled around 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators over the past decade. (Reuters: Rick Wilking)

The vehicles in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks.

"Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA said.

It added that other car makers continued to conduct inflator analysis and testing.

The Honda recall includes certain years of its popular Accord and Civic models. (Reuters)

The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the US.

The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 IS250, 2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner.

The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles.

The Honda recall applies to vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 US states or territories.

Over the past decade, two dozen major car companies have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators worldwide, including about 67 million vehicles in the US.

Metal shrapnel was reportedly unleashed when the airbags exploded. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

Hundreds of injuries in vehicles since 2009 have been reported from Takata airbag inflators that can explode, unleashing metal shrapnel inside cars and trucks.

In some cases, it has killed or injured drivers or other vehicle occupants.

Car company denies liability over airbag incident Toyota Australia says it should not be held liable for traumatic injuries linked to an airbag incident in Darwin.

Honda said long-term monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions.

Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries.

In Australia, Lexus has recalled more than 7,000 vehicles over concerns about Takata airbag inflators that could deteriorate over time.

The recall, announced earlier this month, covers certain Lexus IS250, IS250C, IS350 and IS-F vehicles manufactured between 2005 and 2012. It remains unclear whether other Australian vehicles are affected by the latest global recalls.

Australian motorists can check whether their vehicle is affected through the federal government's Vehicle Recalls website or by contacting their manufacturer.

Owners of recalled vehicles should arrange repairs through an authorised dealer, with replacement of defective airbags carried out free of charge.

Reuters/ABC

title: Authorities investigating four-minute Triple Zero outage in Canberra
text:
Authorities are continuing to investigate a power outage that caused Triple Zero (000) calls in the ACT to inadvertently drop out on Thursday evening.

The outage at the Emergency Services Agency (ESA) headquarters, at Fairbairn near Canberra's airport, lasted four minutes, between 8:11 and 8:15pm on November 19.

In that time, four in-progress ambulance calls cut out, with the ESA saying there were no incoming calls to ambulance or fire and rescue.

Call-centre staff were relocated after the second battery pack took four minutes to kick in. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

ESA Commissioner Wayne Phillips said any attempted calls would have been diverted to ACT Policing, which was not affected.

"I just want to reassure the community that no Triple Zero calls were lost," Commissioner Phillips said.

"We lost a couple at the time but we were able to retrieve them, so the community was never impacted at all through this outage."

Secondary battery pack fails

The drop-out triggered the ESA headquarters' back up battery packs in order to revive the centre.

When the first battery pack failed, the second one took four minutes to kick in.

Commissioner Phillips said he then decided to relocate staff to a back-up centre in Hume, with hopes they would return either late on Saturday night or Sunday morning.

The Transport Workers Union said the failure was a "psychosocial hazard" for those who experienced it. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"What it did show is that our backup systems work really well," he said, referring to the Hume centre.

He said it remained unclear what caused the failure.

"We're still investigating that so at the moment there's some speculation, the speculation might have been lightning or a massive power surge," he said.

'Life and death'

The Transport Workers' Union's Damian Pollard, who represents ambulance workers, called the outage "extremely concerning".

Investigations are continuing into the issue. (ABC News)

"I'd like to thank our members that were on duty that night, [it's] extremely distressing for them, and I could only imagine distressing for the people that were on the call," Mr Pollard said.

"It's also, we have to look at it as, a psychosocial hazard for our members.

"They go above and beyond every shift, that's from every aspect of ACTAS [ACT Ambulance Service]."

title: Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support
text:
Pat Cummins will remain the captain of the Australian cricket team in both the Test and one-day formats after receiving a "unanimous" vote of support from the Cricket Australia board.

His captaincy had been questioned following claims by former Test batters Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft that knowledge of the sandpaper plot during the 2018 South Africa tour was widely known.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met with Cummins in Sydney on Friday, with Cummins saying the meeting "meant a lot" amid the ongoing speculation.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

"Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly," Cummins said in a statement on Saturday.

"David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this, and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins has come under fire for his denials made in a 68-minute press conference on November 13. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cummins encountered several reporters at his house this week after Bancroft broke his silence on the sandpaper saga with a 4,500-word statement.

In the statement, Bancroft said he was left feeling "angry, betrayed and alone" by Cummins's lengthy press conference where he denied any knowledge of sandpaper being brought onto the field.

Among the issues discussed in the meeting between Cummins, Boon and Greenberg were Cummins's welfare and the support required for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn," Boon said in the same CA statement.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon (pictured) says CA "unequivocally" rejects suggestions Cummins's integrity has been compromised. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about, and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there. We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins has been Australia's Test captain since 2021 and is also the captain of the one-day team, having led Australia to the 2023 50-over World Cup title.

title: Bayer to pay $11b over claims weed killer caused cancer
text:
Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $US7.25 billion ($11 billion) over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from US cancer patients, who say the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer, Roundup, could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved by a US judge.

The nationwide settlement handed down on Friday in Missouri applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years.

Participants could get an average of between $US10,000 ($15,000) and $US165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.

For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from US agricultural markets.

Bayer has already changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users.

Bayer's Roundup kills weeds, helping farmers protect crops and improve yields. (Jo Prendergast)

In Australia, all class actions alleging Roundup caused cancer ended without compensation payouts.

In July 2024, the Federal Court dismissed the McNickle case, finding insufficient evidence to establish that glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The remaining Fenton class action was discontinued in January 2025, with no appeal pursued, bringing the Australian litigation to a close.

While the US settlement was pending, the Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits.

Roundup products have been used on weeds since 1974. (AP: Haven Daley)

The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations do not require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labelling requirements.

Though some lawyers for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing, which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.

In a written judgment granting approval, St Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements".

The approved settlement includes $US600 million in legal fees.

Roundup previously contained glyphosate, which Bayer has removed from its new versions. (ABC News: Neale Maude)

The judge said there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected.

Although the decision could be appealed, Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement was "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation".

Bayer announces Roundup alternative After 10 years and hundreds of millions of dollars in research and development, Roundup's owner says it has an alternative.

Roundup has been used on weeds for more than 50 years, with Missouri-based Monsanto debuting Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient.

The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture.

Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer's deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.

The product is also commonly applied on lawns and gardens.

About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens.

As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.

AP/ABC

title: Four people struck by lightning at NSW music festival
text:
Four festivalgoers were struck by lightning and taken to hospital after a severe storm caused chaos at the Strawberry Fields music festival overnight.

The sold-out three-day festival started on Friday on the banks of the Murray River at Tocumwal, on the New South Wales side of the state's border with Victoria.

Ambulance officers took two men to Shepparton Hospital in Victoria while a man and woman were taken to Deniliquin Hospital in NSW.

Festival organisers confirmed they were forced to pause music acts multiple times from Friday afternoon to the early hours of Saturday for safety reasons as crowds sought shelter.

"We can confirm that four people have been transported for further observation and medical checks, all with non-life-threatening injuries; families of those impacted have been contacted," organisers said.

"We wish them a speedy recovery and thank our medical teams, emergency services, and staff for their fast response in enacting our severe weather plan."

Heavy rain, thunder and lightning fell across a large part of northern Victoria on Friday night. (Supplied)

NSW Health said a male, 23, and a female, also 23, were treated at Deniliquin Health Service yesterday and have been discharged.

Vic Health said the two men had also been discharged from Shepparton Hospital.

Social media posts show the festival site inundated with rainwater overnight but organisers said the show would go on.

"We will continue to work with the relevant agencies to monitor conditions closely," they said.

"It appears the worst of the weather has now passed, and we are pleased to confirm the sun is out and the festival will resume normal programming today."

Cricket Australia chairman David Boon wants the latest Sandpapergate saga put to bed before the first Test in Perth, as his board rallied in solidarity behind Pat Cummins following a turbulent fortnight, throwing its unequivocal support behind him to remain captain. The CA board met several times this week to discuss the fallout from Australia’s infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. On Thursday evening the board agreed that there was no reason to reconsider Cummins’ position despite explosive allegations from Cameron Bancroft that everyone in the team knew of the ball-tampering plot eight years ago. Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood during NSW Blues training in Sydney on Thursday. Kate Geraghty Boon flew to Sydney with CA chief executive Todd Greenberg for a meeting on Friday with Cummins and his manager Neil Maxwell at a “private location”, according to the former Australian batsman, to personally convey the board’s unanimous support and check on the welfare of the under-pressure fast bowler. On Saturday, CA confirmed this masthead’s report that Cummins would remain in charge of Australia’s Test team for the opening match of the summer against New Zealand in Perth on December 9.

“[The CA board] chatted it out for quite a considerable amount of time,” Boon told this masthead. “My belief [is] we need solidarity and we need stability. Pat has without a doubt over the last five years been an outstanding leader and he has been a focal point of a rebuild of the culture in the Australian cricket team. “We saw absolutely no reason to reconsider his role. Every single board member backs his leadership and integrity. We know there are things that have got to happen for it to be finally put to bed and we are trying to ensure that occurs over the next short period of time. Hopefully, it settles down right now before the first Test starts in Perth.” Central to that process is the establishment of an independent forum, announced by CA earlier this week, to allow players and staff involved in the 2018 tour to give their accounts of what happened. Further details are expected in the coming days, with several prominent players indicating their willingness to participate.

Cummins confirmed on Saturday, in a statement released by CA, that he would attend the forum and share his recollections of 2018, which differ from accounts given by the likes of Usman Khawaja, David Warner, Bancroft and Chadd Sayers. “I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there,” Cummins said. “All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Loading “Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority. “It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly.”

Boon said the willingness of Cummins, Khawaja and Bancroft to participate was encouraging, but all eyes will be on whether Warner attends. “I think that’s a great show of faith in the process that we’re establishing,” Boon said. “We’re extremely respectful of all opinions and all views. It’s up to us to take responsibility, take ownership, and sort this out as best we possibly can with the interests of Australian cricket at the forefront of mind.” Pat Cummins answered questions for well over an hour. Sam Mooy Boon admitted he had been saddened by the events of the past fortnight and said player welfare was a major consideration behind Friday’s meeting with Cummins, who has had reporters stationed outside his Sydney home. Other members of the 2018 team, including Steve Smith, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, have also found themselves under scrutiny as fresh questions emerge about what happened in South Africa. The bowlers’ accounts differ from Bancroft, Khawaja and Warner.

“They’re all feeling the pressure,” Boon said. “What we think is paramount in anything like this is the welfare of our players – not only Pat – but the rest of the team and expressing the fact that we support them in every way. “Our support for the whole team is unequivocally strong and this includes supporting Steve Smith, Mitch Marsh, all the team members, and the staff.” Asked if Cummins had indicated he wanted to remain Test captain, Boon said: “Yeah, I sensed that. I think Pat is extremely proud to be the Australian captain and he wants to continue to do that. “We want Australian cricket to be what it should be. That’s a national sport for everybody and the pride of the nation. The game needs to unite. It needs to move on together and we need to do everything in our power to make that happen.” The announcement of Australia’s Test squad for the New Zealand series has been delayed amid the controversy – that is expected some time next week after the upcoming round of Sheffield Shield – while some players have been shielded from facing the media as CA attempts to contain the fallout.

Despite the turmoil, and Australia’s 2-1 series defeat in South Africa last month, Boon is confident the team will be ready for the opening Test in Perth. “We’re in a position with the support that’s provided, the talent that we have, that we can move forward and be ready to play by that time,” he said. Loading It comes as Hazlewood broke his silence over the ball-tampering scandal and launched a strong defence of Cummins. Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood rejected suggestions that Australia’s bowling attack knew about the use of sandpaper during the third Test against South Africa, insisting he had no involvement in, or knowledge of, any plan to alter the condition of the ball.

Australian cricket Pat Cummins is under siege. His manager blames ‘hysteria unfounded in reality’ Hazlewood said while he was sympathetic about the “ridiculous” suspensions Bancroft, Smith and Warner received for their part in the scandal, there was a distinction between assuming teammates knew about the ball-tampering operation and having actual knowledge of it. “Assuming everyone knows and actually knowing everyone knows – that gap is huge. That’s a big chasm,” Hazlewood said. His comments come after Bancroft reignited the controversy through a recent column detailing his recollections of the scandal and questioning the extent of the bowling group’s knowledge.

Hazlewood acknowledged that Australia’s team environment was fractured at the time, with divisions between batsmen and bowlers contributing to a toxic dressing-room culture. But he rejected claims that the entire team was aware of what was happening. “No [I had no knowledge of ball tampering taking place in that series]. We were interviewed straight after [Cape Town] and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after,” Hazlewood said. “It was fresh in my mind at that point. Two things stand out for me from what’s been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? “The answer is no. When it boils down to it, I think those two points are crucial.” The experienced fast bowler also threw his support behind Cummins, praising the Australian captain for transforming the team’s culture following the events of 2018.

He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.” Hazlewood went on to warn that stripping Cummins of the captaincy would plunge the Australian team into turmoil. When pressed on whether he might walk away from the Test team in protest, he conceded it was a scenario he would carefully weigh. “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah,” he said.

Addressing the original allegations, Hazlewood insisted he had no knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper, including suggestions that those discussions took place in the Port Elizabeth dressing room before Bancroft carried out the act. Tea breaks, he said, were generally busy periods for bowlers, who were preparing their equipment and getting back onto the field, often without engaging in conversations among other players. “As bowlers in a tea break. You’ve only got 20 minutes, so I’m probably changing all my gear, and I’m getting out on the field earlier to bowl to whoever wants to catch, probably the fielding coach,” he said. “It’s a lot different to lunch where you sit down and touch on things about how the game is going. Tea breaks are a very busy time.” Hazlewood also dismissed suggestions that bowlers should have recognised the ball had been illegally altered. A townhouse opposite Studley Park in Kew cast a spell over a local mother, who paid $2.11 million at auction and hit the reserve with her bullish first bid. The three-bedroom home at 1/10 Walmer Street last sold 26 years ago, and the underbidder from that sale came to watch the auction on Saturday. They didn’t bid, but told agent Sam Tilley from Nelson Alexander Kew they had “always regretted missing out on it”. title: Threats, insults, settlements: How Jensen Huang made humiliation routine

As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before US House politicians on his relationship with Alice Huang. Getty Images This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain”. The tirades were a centrepiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $US5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. ‘You have to do this, or I will rip your f---ing heart out and stomp on it.’ Alleged remark by Jensen Huang “I’d rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,” he once said.

Advertisement

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behaviour kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Related Article Trump's America ‘Vibes have definitely shifted’: The perfect storm that changed how America sees big tech Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear. Huang’s behaviour began long before Nvidia became one of the world’s most valuable companies. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behaviour” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $US1 million, which has not been previously reported. ‘I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!’ Former Nvidia executive Michael Winston on Jensen Huang

Advertisement

Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom US intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, according to six current and former employees, including his own daughter, Madison, who, as his de facto chief of staff, often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Former senior vice president of human resources at Nvidia Michael Winston. He died earlier this year. NYT Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesperson, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behaviour. Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mould of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Huang once belittled Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Harvey Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said last week that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It pained me’

Advertisement

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organisational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the AI boom. President Donald Trump has said reinstating Nvidia’s former chief executive “certainly isn’t a bad idea”. AP Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behaviour was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the HR department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by the Times. In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.

Advertisement

That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Winston said Huang unleashed graphic violent threats. “You have to do this, or I will rip your f---ing heart out and stomp on it,” Huang said at one point. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Lawyer up, Elon. Your astronomical greed and power is about to be exposed Robert Reich Professor “I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston said other attendees were “terrorised” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up”. Winston said he then confronted Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage”. Winston said Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it. Winston said Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Huang told him.

title: A grieving father took on the government over hotel quarantine. He’s not keeping a cent of the settlement
text:

He’s not keeping a cent of the settlement Erin Pearson November 21, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Once every three months, Hayden Flinn sits down to dinner with four other fathers who have all lost a child. He carries a membership to a club he never wished to join – one that has changed his life forever. They speak about youth mental health and of grief and of ways to make the world a better place for the young people of the future. Flinn knows pain, having lost his young teenage daughter suddenly in May 2021 following her battle with mental health. But the Hong Kong-based corporate lawyer says he also knows injustice when he sees it. Hayden Flinn and his wife Dr Sarah Whorlow. Simon Schluter This week, he took the Victorian government to the Supreme Court and won a confidential settlement on the eve of a 10-day trial, claiming he had been unlawfully detained in hotel quarantine for two weeks after his 13-year-old girl died in Melbourne during the coronavirus pandemic.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Courts A father’s rage over daughter’s death has smouldered since lockdown – Brett Sutton is in his sights At the time, in May 2021, there were no local transmissions in Melbourne and the country he was travelling from was not on the government list of virus danger zones. When he landed in Melbourne, Flinn, a co-chief executive of a large Hong Kong law firm, was bussed to a small Richmond hotel room with his teenage son after the pair were refused permission to quarantine at home with family. Flinn filed a lawsuit against the state and its Health Department in 2024, claiming he had been unnecessarily detained for two weeks when he was subjected to indignity and insult, a loss of liberty and mental distress when he was refused an exemption to hotel quarantine on compassionate grounds. At a time when he says he should have been viewing his daughter’s body and helping his wife plan the funeral, he was trapped in hotel quarantine. He argued he should never have been detained, with officials failing to properly assess his personal circumstances, vaccination status and the low risk presented by travellers from Hong Kong.

Advertisement

“It was a difficult time,” he told this masthead. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Hotel quarantine back on trial at worst possible time for Carroll Alex King, partner at King and Collins law firm, estimates the state would have spent in excess of $2 million in taxpayer funds defending its case had the case gone to court. When he met Flinn for the first time, King recalls coming across a meticulously prepared father, who arrived at King’s office with an abundance of material. “The one thing that struck me with Hayden is, sometimes you have a conference with a client and to be frank, you don’t need to prepare that much. Whenever you have a conference with Hayden you have to prepare because you know he’ll be better prepared, and that’s not a good look,” King says.

Advertisement

“That became a feature and ... really just showed me Hayden was completely resolute and driven about this case. “There seemed to be this unquenchable, inexhaustible fire behind all of this which probably came from a number of sources but one of them was … the large expatriate community in Hong Kong, I think about 100,000 people. Hayden would say to me that it had been said to him, ‘if you can’t do this, who can?’.” But what followed, King says, was stonewalling from government departments, including those that manage freedom of information requests. COVID-19 testing at Melbourne’s showgrounds in 2020. Bloomberg “We realised we then had to move fairly quickly because of the three-year limitations period on bringing a tort of false imprisonment. There was a lack of public information, and while Hayden had started digging around, governments are like vaults, they just won’t give stuff away, notwithstanding the FOI [freedom of information] regimes,” King says.

Advertisement

“There was an enormous amount of work done over that ensuing year that when he did a lot of FOI requests to Commonwealth and Victorian agencies, we were continually rebuffed.” King says when the government’s pleadings were finally filed, they revealed the decision by then-chief health officer Brett Sutton to hold Flinn in hotel quarantine had never even been written down. If it were not for Flinn’s discipline and courage and energy to uncover the truth, King says the state might never have settled, pausing to acknowledge it was a massive enterprise to take on the government, with the loser of court proceedings facing the prospect of paying both parties’ legal costs. Passengers disembark from a chartered flight from Uruguay after being evacuated off the coronavirus-stricken Greg Mortimer cruise ship. Getty “In court proceedings for false imprisonment, the usual position is wanting money in damages for that false imprisonment. As part of his settlement with the state, though, Hayden sought no financial compensation. He did not want a dollar for his pocket,” King says.

Advertisement

Related Article Mental health Victoria has the most kids in crisis, but the state government refused a $4.5m funding plea What he wanted, King says, was justice. Flinn is donating every cent received from the government to help young people struggling with mental health. For Flinn’s wife Sarah Whorlow, 2021 is a time she struggles to talk about. Battling to get her husband out of hotel quarantine to be with his grieving family was horrific, she says. She hopes her family can now focus on helping other families in need and spreading awareness of youth mental health. “[I was] needing to deal with coroners and police and funeral homes and cemeteries while he was locked up, that was very challenging,” she says.

Advertisement

“I don’t think Hayden could’ve got through all of this without ... the support ... of friends and lawyers.” Related Article Editorial

Tragedy No excuses. Review of youth mental health services is needed now The Age's View Editorial In a statement signed by Secretary of Health Jenny Atta, seen by this masthead, she says the state regrets the impact that mandatory hotel quarantine had on Flinn’s family, but denies any allegation of wrongdoing. “The state acknowledges that Mr Flinn’s detention caused him and his family significant personal distress and regrets this,” Atta says. “At Mr Flinn’s request, the state has agreed to make a monetary contribution to be used by Mr Flinn for charitable purposes focussing on Victorian youth mental health.”

Advertisement

Hugh de Kretser, the president of the Australian Human Rights Commission, thanked Flinn for bringing his case and ensuring some accountability for the detention decisions that impacted many others in similar circumstances. “Your actions will help to ensure a more compassionate and humane response to future public health emergencies,” de Kretser says. Flinn and Whorlow plan to now take some time to find the right charity for them, one they hope to work with long term and where they can share their own lived experience of youth mental health when the time feels right. They also hope to bring attention to better solutions for helping children in mental health crisis, rather than busy, bright and loud emergency departments like those that their daughter visited before she died.

Advertisement

A close family friend, who asked not to be named, says there remains a generation of young people who lost their social networks during the pandemic and who are finding it difficult to rebuild those. “What is disturbing is the number of suicides that are happening in the community and they’re getting younger. It’s the leading cause of death in people aged 15 to 24 in Australia, and I think it astounds most people,” Flinn says. NRL players believe their season is too long, while their NRLW counterparts feel theirs is too short, according to a survey of almost 1000 players across both competitions. The Rugby League Players’ Association is finalising the results of its annual Player Pulse survey, which provides a snapshot of their views across various topics. Roosters ironman Siua Wong has played more than 30 games in 2026. Getty Images This year there were 969 respondents – 600 from the NRL and 369 from the NRLW – with at least 80 per cent of top contracted players from each club taking part. While the full results are a week away from being released, one of the intriguing early findings was the reaction to the length of the season. The topic is timely, given the NRL only released its draw for 2027 on Friday.

As far as NRL players are concerned, their season is too long; 37 per cent of respondents recorded their satisfaction with the NRL season length 5 or below out of 10. Only 12 per cent of NRL players rated very or extremely high their satisfaction with the season length. As for the NRLW players surveyed, 44 per cent of NRLW players rated their satisfaction with the season length as 5 or below out of 10. The 2026 season was a particularly long one for players who participated in the World Cup. For instance, Tongan forward Siua Wong played two trials, 27 club matches for the premiership-winning Roosters and four internationals, taking his season total to 33. Wong is one of several players who have also played more than 30 games in what is becoming an increasingly demanding schedule, particularly during World Cup years.

While male players have between seven and nine weeks of annual leave, depending on their level of experience, 48 per cent of those surveyed felt pressure to return to training early. NRL 2027 Every team’s 2027 draw ranked – why the Bears are cheering and rivals left crying “As the NRL and NRLW seasons become more demanding, physically and mentally, and travel commitments are expected to increase in the coming years, especially for the men and women who play rep football, mandatory time off gives players the chance to rest, recover, and spend time with family,” said Penrith playmaker Jack Cogger, who is a member of the RLPA board. “This ensures they’re in the best position to back up year after year and deliver their best for clubs and fans next season.”

North Melbourne outlasted a valiant Sydney to book their place in a fourth consecutive grand final, storming to a 32-point victory in front of a roaring crowd at Ikon Park, 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51). A global Ticketmaster outage initially wrought havoc on Saturday’s AFLW preliminary final double-header, with long queues of frustrated footy fans left waiting to get into the stadium midway through the first quarter. The Swans got off to a blistering start, with Cynthia Hamilton booting the game’s opening goal in just 21 seconds – one of the fastest opening goals in AFLW history. Backed by a roaring blue-and-white crowd, the North juggernaut kicked into gear, with Jasmine Garner kick-starting a string of goals. Suddenly, the Swans were in trouble, staring down the barrel of a 36-point deficit in the second term. But, just like in last week’s breathtaking final against Geelong, Swans superstar Chloe Molloy was a telling standout. Molloy kicked her first goal of the game in the second term, becoming the first player in AFLW history to kick 20 goals in a seven-game stretch, breaking the record of 19 set by Aishling Moloney in 2024. Tensions flared in the second quarter after Roos veteran Emma Kearney (a columnist for this masthead) was caught holding the ball, giving away a free kick to Molloy, who converted. When the star Swan celebrated, Keaney ran up to mock celebrate alongside the Sydney crew, with a few jumper grabs and push and shoves included for good measure. It only seemed to inspire Molloy, who kicked her third consecutive goal moments later. After another pivotal goal from Hamilton in the third, the Swans found themselves within 12 points of the Roos and with all the momentum. A soccer-like goal from Blaithin Bogue kept the two-time reigning premiers ahead, but the Swans hit back with a goal in the opening minute of the final term from young star Maddie Quinn. Emma Kearney assesses her options down the ground in North’s clash with Sydney. AFL Photos As the clock ticked down, both sides wrestled for momentum and amped up the pressure. But, seemingly as always, the Roos remained one step ahead, with Garner and Bella Eddey slotting goals to extinguish Sydney’s hopes of a maiden grand final berth.

Swans coach Colin O’Riordan said while the result was a disappointing one for his group, he was proud of their ability to face adversity throughout the season – on-field and off. “[We’re] pretty disappointed, that’s a given,” he said. “You’ve just lost a brilliant final, so yeah, the group is shattered.” Kearney was at her hard-nosed best for the Roos, while league medallist Ash Riddell finished with a game-high 29 touches to go with her seven clearances and 337 metres gained. The Blues take on Melbourne in the second match of the Ikon Park preliminary final double-header. The victors will face the Roos in the grand final on Friday night.

We’ll have a good look at those, but for us, it’ll be what does our best footy look like? … We have a great opportunity to try to bring that best football one more time for this season.” Ahead of Monday night’s AFLW best-and-fairest award count, Crocker was asked about Garner’s chances of taking out the top gong. Despite being one of the best players in the competition, the 32-year-old has never won the league’s highest honour, losing out to teammate Riddell last year.

The Coalition has vowed to keep VicHealth as a standalone agency if it forms government after next Saturday’s election, rejecting Labor’s plan to wind it up in a move that has won the support of public health leaders. A Wilson government would also seek to shift the focus of the internationally renowned preventative health body away from social causes and onto the state’s most pressing public health challenges, such as obesity and falling vaccination rates. Burnet Institute research scientist Lilian Hor (left) speaks to opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson. Eddie Jim The commitment to keep VicHealth as an independent, statutory authority rather than fold it into the health department was endorsed by the Australian Medical Association, the Public Health Association of Australia, and some of the state’s leading public health advocates. Australia’s most renowned immunologist Sir Gustav Nossal, University of Melbourne professor of public health Rob Moodie and renowned epidemiologist Fiona Stanley on Wednesday wrote personally to Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, thanking the Coalition for its “principled stand in opposing the abolition of VicHealth”.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Bone-headed decision’: Government under pressure to spare VicHealth from axe The three scientists also wrote to Premier Ben Carroll and urged him to reconsider his government’s decision to wind up the 40-year-old institution. “Every serious modern review of health promotion – including work by the OECD and WHO – has concluded that statutory independence and secure long-term funding are the two conditions on which effective prevention most depends,” they wrote. “VicHealth was designed with both features, including its pioneering hypothecated funding model, which deliberately protects prevention spending from short-term fiscal pressures. “Trading a structural protection of that kind for a one-off saving is, on any reasonable long-run costing, a poor bargain for the Victorian budget as much as for public health outcomes.”

Advertisement

The scientists urged Carroll, who since becoming premier has reversed significant policies of his predecessors, to consider the “final, poignant plea” by the late Tim Read, a general practitioner, Greens MP and public health champion, to protect VicHealth. Sir Gustav was the inaugural chair of VicHealth and Professor Moodie previously served as its chief executive. The late Greens MP Tim Read used his last speech in parliament to advocate for VicHealth. Simon Schluter The Carroll government was dismissive of the Coalition commitment to keep VicHealth. “Jess Wilson is going to fund a bunch of bureaucrats and then cut thousands of nurses leaving Victorians worse off,” a Labor Party spokesperon said.

Advertisement

An enduring legacy of the Cain government, the preventative health agency has been in limbo since the end of last year when the government accepted a recommendation by Helen Silver’s review of the public service to wind it up as a standalone entity and absorb its functions into the Department of Health. The Liberal Party opposed the change at the time and pledged to vote against any legislation designed to dismantle VicHealth, which was established and funded through provisions in the state’s tobacco laws. Opposition health spokesperson Georgie Crozier warned that absorbing VicHealth and its ring-fenced $45 million funding into a $30 billion department would see its work disappear into a bureaucratic black hole. In response to questions from The Age last week, a Liberal Party spokesperson made clear that under a Coalition government, VicHealth would remain an independent statutory authority.

Advertisement

“The Liberals and Nationals have committed to retaining VicHealth,” they said. “We recognise the importance of its independence and the valuable role it has played in improving the health and wellbeing of Victorians. Related Article Opinion

Healthcare There’s a simple calculation about health that should outrage anyone who can do arithmetic Chip Le Grand State political editor “VicHealth has a proud history of leading public health campaigns and encouraging healthier lifestyles. We want to see that work continue, particularly as we confront the growing burden of preventable chronic disease. “With an ageing and growing population, and more Victorians living with chronic disease, we can’t afford to treat preventative health as an afterthought.” The Coalition also pledged to retain the local public health units (LPHUs) established at the height of Victoria’s pandemic response. These units, which operate within city and regional hospitals, were an attempt to improve a public health system which, when compared to NSW and Queensland, was under-resourced and too centralised.

Advertisement

The Liberal spokesperson said LPHUs played a “vital role” in dispensing vaccines, providing advice and responding to outbreaks of measles and other communicable disease. A senior Coalition figure said that under a Wilson government, VicHealth would be asked to devote less time and fewer resources to social issues such as violence against women and racism, and more on core public health messaging. AMA Victoria president Simon Judkins and Public Health Association of Australia chief Terry Slevin welcomed the commitment to keep VicHealth quarantined from the broader health bureaucracy. Australian Medical Association Victorian president Simon Judkins during the doctors’ strike in October. title: Bancroft never had a chance in the Test arena. In a bitter irony, Warner stood in his way
text:

SportCricketBall tampering Opinion Bancroft never had a chance in the Test arena. In a bitter irony, Warner stood in his way Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist November 21, 2026 — 1:30pm

November 21, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“My cricket career has been destroyed, and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.” The story of Cameron Bancroft’s Test cricket career, and how it intertwined with David Warner’s, is one of the most fascinating intrigues of the Sandpapergate saga. Cameron Bancroft Test career was never the same after the sandpaper scandal in South Africa in 2018. Sports Inc In time, the mystery will be given due attention, and Bancroft’s what-if may be answered. Bancroft came into the Australian Test team for the 2017-18 Ashes when, aged 25, he replaced Matthew Renshaw to partner Warner, who was then at his peak and vice-captain of the team.

Advertisement

Bancroft played every match until he was banned for using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town in 2018, making two half-centuries, almost but not quite bedding down his spot. After his ban, he returned for the first two Tests of the 2019 Ashes series in England, but after scores of 8, 7, 13 and 16 he was dropped for Marcus Harris. Cameron Bancroft walks off after his dismissal at Lord’s in an Ashes Test in 2019. It would be his last appearance for Australia in a Test match. AP He has never played Test cricket again. After Warner’s retirement in 2024, Bancroft’s form did not warrant a recall.

Advertisement

The interesting period is between 2020 and 2024, when Bancroft dominated the Sheffield Shield, when Australia was desperate for regeneration at the top of the order, when Warner was continually failing, and yet Bancroft was not chosen. When he talks about his cricket career being “destroyed”, this is the key period. Cameron Bancroft celebrates a ton for Western Australia in the Sheffield Shield final against Victoria in March 2022. Getty Images Across these seasons, Bancroft was the highest overall Shield run-scorer and easily the highest run-scorer among openers. In the Australian team, Usman Khawaja was enjoying his late-career renaissance as an opener, and his selection was never in question.

Advertisement

At the other end, in these same four years, Warner played 28 matches for Australia, averaged 31.46 and scored two centuries. His highest Test average in any full season was 34.00. The only time he averaged 40 in a Test series was at home against South Africa in 2022-23 when his scores were 0, 3, 200 and 10. Bancroft’s Sheffield Shield statistics over four seasons (2020-2024) 2020-21: 541 runs, 1 century, average 49.18 2021-22: 502 runs, 2 centuries, average 35.85 2022-23: 945 runs, 4 centuries, average 59.06 2023-24: 778 runs, 3 centuries, average 48.62 It looked strange. Were the selectors not watching the Sheffield Shield? Did they have something against Bancroft? George Bailey was a selector for the entire period, with Andrew McDonald replacing Langer in 2021 and Tony Dodemaide coming in that same year to replace Trevor Hohns. Greg Chappell had been a selector earlier in the period, before Warner’s form became a concern.

Advertisement

His dip seemed pressing by 2022, though, when Warner had gone nearly three years and 28 innings with no centuries and four 50s. After his 200 against South Africa in Melbourne that December, he went another year and 16 innings before another ton. His average nosedived. There were widening calls for Warner to be dropped and for Australia to bring in new blood. David Warner had a run of outs but managed to hold his place in the Australian Test team until his retirement. Getty Bancroft seemed to be that option as he was the one piling on Shield runs. It was an intriguing relationship. Bancroft had volunteered to cheat with sandpaper in South Africa when Warner thought he would be under too much scrutiny. He had followed Warner’s instructions on how to cheat. But now, when Bancroft was making century after century for Western Australia, Warner was saying there were no Test-quality openers around.

Advertisement

Throughout this period, Warner’s manager James Erskine repeatedly alluded to Warner knowing more about Sandpapergate than he’d let on. Warner never disputed or shut down Erskine’s veiled threats and Erskine remained his manager. It has now turned out – via Khawaja and Bancroft – that these allusions contained more than a grain of truth. Former Test batsman Cameron Bancroft and ex-opener David Warner have had an intriguing relationship over the years. Getty Images Warner did have dirt on the Australian bowlers. And he had loyalists to dish it out for him. Through 2023, even after he was injured and left the tour to India, after a moderate Ashes series in England (averaging 27.41), Warner was allowed to stay in the team until he decided to retire on his timetable, at the Sydney Test against Pakistan in 2024.

Advertisement

Selectors, with a chronic shortage of Test-fit openers and top-order batters, must still be regretting giving Warner his long period of grace. Or are they? Warner was under no obligation to make way for Bancroft or anyone else in 2022 or 2023. He was entitled to push for everything he got, and he was motivated by his grievance over the heavy punishment he received for the Newlands episode. It wasn’t for him to retire; it was for the selectors to stop picking him. Now the truth is coming out, the question I would like to see pursued is whether the threat posed by Warner’s knowledge of the sandpaper cover-up played any role in the selectors’ decisions to keep on picking him when he was ageing and failing and the batting needed regeneration.

Advertisement

Another perspective Opinion

Ball tampering We need to deal with Sandpapergate before the 150th anniversary Test Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain Were there any communications between anyone at Cricket Australia and the selectors on this issue? Were there any communications between Warner and the selectors about it? Bailey, during his short Test career, had been an admiring minor teammate of Warner’s, and as a selector he chose to frequent the changing room and wear team apparel, almost as if he was still a member. Were there any discussions among the selectors about Warner’s knowledge of the Sandpapergate cover-up, and did they have any impact on selections? Selection discussions are meant to be confidential. But this is an issue directly related to Sandpapergate, and one which Bancroft has raised. It needs to be asked. In time, it may be answered. Bancroft may or may not have had a successful Test career, but he never got a chance because, in a bitter irony, Warner stood in his way.

title: A Wallabies captain was told he’d be back from injury in 10 days. It took two years
text:
Advertisement

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby A Wallabies captain was told he’d be back from injury in 10 days. It took two years Iain Payten November 21, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Twenty-nine months ago, Liam Wright was living his dream. It was the middle of 2024, and the Queensland flanker had not only been recalled to the Wallabies after a long absence, but then-coach Joe Schmidt had also made him the skipper. Wright was just the 98th man to hold the role in 137 years, and an exciting period, including a Lions tour and a home World Cup, lay ahead. Liam Wright posing after being named as Wallabies captain in 2024. Getty Images Wright led the Wallabies to a win over Wales in Sydney but a regulation tackle late in the game saw him injure his right shoulder. The initial diagnosis was he would be back in 10 days. It took two years.

Advertisement

“The hardest part was that it went from the absolute high of captaining your country, and getting back into the Test setup for the first time in four years, to a lot of uncertainty,” Wright said. But now, after enduring an agonising stretch of trial-and-error with an injury that confounded doctors, required four surgeries and many aborted comebacks, and ultimately led to the end of his time at the Reds, Wright is back on the field and loving life again. Wallabies players at the Ospreys (from left): Liam Wright, Marika Koroibete, Lalakai Foketi and Ryan Smith. Iain Payten It has taken a move to the other side of the world, with Wright having recently relaunched his career at the Ospreys club, in Wales. He is one of five Australians at the Swansea-based URC franchise, along with Ryan Smith, and other recent arrivals Marika Koroibete, Lalakai Foketi and Lawson Creighton. There are now so many people speaking with a broad Australian accent at the club, local media has taken to calling it “Ospreylia”.

Advertisement

Wright opened up with travelling Australian media on the turmoil of his journey, his joy at returning and why, despite still harbouring a desire to play for the Wallabies, he would also be open to representing Wales at the World Cup. “The main thing for coming over here was just to really try something different,” Wright said. “I had a difficult end to my time in Australia … so I was looking to just get a fresh opportunity, leave some of that baggage behind me.” Liam Wright winning a lineout for the Wallabies against Wales in 2024. Getty Images The simple version of Wright’s injury was that his shoulder would persistently lock up and lose function. The reason it was happening was puzzling and complex. “It wasn’t clear-cut from the beginning that this is going to be a long layoff,” he said.

Advertisement

“The initial diagnosis was, ‘Oh mate, a little bit of a frozen shoulder, we should have you right in 10 days to play that Georgia Test.’ We genuinely thought, ‘All right, a couple more weeks, we’ll aim for the Springboks Test,’ or ‘We’ll aim for the All Blacks Test’. And then little setback after little setback, it just kind of kept losing motor function. “[Wallabies doctor Gary Mitchell] still reckons it’s the toughest case he’s had to crack, in terms of just there was no real rhyme or reason to why it would or wouldn’t work. Liam Wright, playing for Ospreys, takes the ball in line out playing for his Welsh club last month. Getty Images “I’d get a real innocuous hit and essentially just couldn’t lift my arm off my chest. But structurally, the scans were showing everything is positive.” With varying diagnoses, Wright attempted multiple treatment paths, pushing to be back for the British and Irish Lions tour in 2025.

Advertisement

He returned for the Reds for two games in March that year, but then missed the rest of the season. More surgeries followed. Even for a driven player like Wright, there were many dark days. The 29-year-old didn’t want to retire, but the word did float around him. Wright said the support of his fiancée Sara kept him afloat. “My missus was fantastic. We just made a rule where it’s ‘We don’t quit on a bad day’,” Wright said. “And so it wasn’t an option for me. I knew I could get back to playing good footy, but I understand the way it had to kind of end in Australia as well.” Wright’s contract with the Reds wasn’t extended after 2025, but after surgery on a labral tear and a long-term strengthening program finally worked, he got back in Brisbane club rugby in June 2026, for boyhood club Easts.

Advertisement

Through Ryan Smith, his former Reds teammate who joined the Ospreys in 2025 and has acted as a green-and-gold recruitment officer for all the Aussies who’ve followed, Wright ended up taking an offer to head to Wales, with Sara. He has been outstanding in his five games for the Ospreys, to the point that local media have raised the prospect of him switching allegiances to Wales when a three-year international stand-down would expire in July. Wales coach Steve Tandy has said he would consider it. Wright – who qualifies for Wales via a grandfather born in Pembroke – is open-minded, but a catch-up with the Wallabies in Cardiff on Wednesday appears to have fanned his flame about wearing gold again. Wright and the other Ospreylians have plans to be at Principality Stadium for the Wallabies-Wales clash on Sunday, all wearing gold. “Test footy is what I want to be playing. I imagine myself doing it in a gold jersey and I want to do it for the gold jersey, but I’m not going to turn down opportunities anywhere,” Wright said.

Advertisement

“If the door’s closed for the Wallabies and I’m playing good enough footy to play Test footy and Wales do come knocking, then I’d definitely explore it. Could Liam Wright return to the Wallabies? Getty Images “But I went down to visit some of the boys yesterday, they’re running a real nice tight ship there. “They haven’t quite got the results just yet, but I know what Kissie can do in a short time and I know he puts a lot of care in, so when things start to develop it can happen quickly. “I want to get back playing Test footy. I want to play for the Wallabies, but fate has a weird way of working. We’ve landed in Wales with heritage I’ve now got to explore.

Advertisement

“I was going past Pembroke Dock the other week and stayed there in a nice Airbnb and explored the area a bit, which is where my grandfather’s from, and so things have a funny way of working out.” ‘Test footy is what I want to be playing. I imagine myself doing it in a gold jersey.’ Liam Wright Wright doesn’t have the flashy running game of other Wallabies, but brings immense value as a lineout technician, a leader and a tireless breakdown worker. It is an industrious profile that the Wallabies are short on, as had been exposed on their spring tour. Asked if he was still interested in Wright for the Wallabies, Kiss said: “The big thing for Liam was just getting back into the game.” Related Article Australian rugby Infamous MCG moment won’t drive Tizzano as he faces Lions nemesis in Wales

Advertisement

“I’ve worked closely with him at the Reds for a number of years and he was in that gym, in the physio room, throwing everything to get that shoulder right,” Kiss said. “I just loved the look in his eyes, you know? He looked really happy again getting out there, plying his trade, loving the sense of living in a different environment, all those things. “So we’ll keep an eye on him and Lawson and all the others that are in Europe at the moment. But I was really happy to see him and catch up with him and see how he feels really good about himself again. “And someone of his calibre, we’ll keep an eye on for sure.”
