Australia’s all-star bowling contingent has achieved greatness, but attention is turning to who will fill their places when they’re gone. The nation will play as many as 16 Tests from December to July, and there is no guarantee the ensemble of Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Scott Boland, Michael Neser and Nathan Lyon will push on beyond the 2027 Ashes. Cummins is the youngest at 33. A home summer against New Zealand will be followed by tours to India and England, a 150th anniversary clash against the Old Enemy, and potentially a World Test Championship final. The ongoing sandpaper saga – from Usman Khawaja’s revelations in his book Sabr to Cameron Bancroft’s explosive column – clouds the future further. The battle to replace the likes of Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins (left) is heated, with Xavier Bartlett and Riley Meredith (right) among the contenders. Getty We break down and rank the men eager to press their claims as the country’s successors.

Advertisement

The quicks: Secret weapon behind next spearhead The prospect of Xavier Bartlett pushing to earn a Baggy Green this summer has taken a nose dive, with his latest injury setback coming after one former international quick lauded him as the man to succeed Australia’s all-conquering veteran spearheads. Despite 19-year-old Mahli Beardman being the man of the hour last week when he claimed 6-21 on his one-day debut for the country, Bartlett was unveiled as the leader of a young attack. While expensive in Australia’s two defeats, his five wickets – trailing only Beardman and Gus Atkinson – came as a wicket-taker in each contest. Loading Before revelations emerged that Bartlett had been withdrawn from the nation’s T20 squad to battle England in five clashes beginning on Saturday night, due to a knee injury, Hamish Bennett – who represented New Zealand 31 times across all three formats, and now serves as the Bulls’ bowling coach – believed he had already announced himself as ready for a Test call-up as early as the forthcoming series against New Zealand.

Advertisement

Next year’s Ashes campaign and England’s swing-friendly conditions are tipped to favour the Queenslander’s strengths if he can turn his purple patch of form – which includes 16 wickets from two Sheffield Shield clashes this summer – into a maiden Test squad selection. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Baby Barrel’: The next Boland leading Australia’s emerging cartel Bartlett will be subject to further assessment before a return timeline is planned. Beardman has also been removed from the T20 international squad due to a low-grade quadriceps train, and is expected to make his comeback during the Big Bash League for the Perth Scorchers. Opportunities for Shield matches have been scarce for Bartlett, who managed just three caps last summer. But Bennett told this masthead before Bartlett joined the ODI camp that a rare period to play in back-to-back contests in October had demonstrated the Gold Coast product was ready to shine with the red ball. “I’m sure he’s one of those names now that [national selector] George Bailey and the likes are talking about, and whether he can be a chance of playing in the New Zealand series or not,” Bennett said.

Advertisement

“He’s come into these two games unrestricted and been able to play a full part in the fixtures, and we saw that when we can call on him at any time he delivers. “He’s showing how skillful he is, and the way he trains and prepares has probably been the most impressive thing about Xav – those little things in how he warms up, how he preps to bowl and how he goes about it. “He’s pretty resilient, he’s had some really good exposure through international white ball cricket and franchise leagues, and that definitely helps develop your craft. You’d have to seriously consider him … his red ball skills are just going to get better and better.” Xavier Bartlett in action for Australia. Getty Images The prospect of an Ashes berth was put to Bartlett ahead of the ODI series against England.

Advertisement

“An Ashes series is a massive opportunity. It’s there, but I don’t want to look too far ahead,” Bartlett said. “If I can put some good performances on the board I’ll be in and around that conversation.” Bartlett said Bennett had been a secret weapon in his rise, and that of Neser ahead of the latter’s breakout 2025-26 summer (15 wickets from three Tests). “A big thing for me [was] trying to keep my ball speed up, trying to stay consistently around the mid-130s for me to try and have a bit more of an effect, especially when the ball stops swinging and seaming, and trying to take some wickets in the middle overs,” Bartlett said.

Advertisement

“Hamish has been awesome. This is his second year with Queensland, and he did some really good stuff with Nes before the Ashes to keep his ball speed up, and we saw the rewards.” The spinners: Frontrunner to succeed Lyon Matthew Kuhnemann admits the thought of returning to India is hard to ignore, but he has rubbished suggestions he will fill Nathan Lyon’s shoes before the “GOAT’s” career is finished. At a time when the future of Australia’s spin bowling has been scrutinised following Lyon being left out of the side three times within 15 months in favour of an all-pace attack, Kuhnemann sensed change was afoot ahead of January’s subcontinent tour. Nathan Lyon and Matthew Kuhnemann. Getty Images

Advertisement

Related Article Test cricket ‘Doesn’t change my focus’: Possible Labuschagne successor thrives in spotlight While the 30-year-old believed some pitches were being tailored towards games going for the full four days, presenting more chances for spinners to shine, his figures of 4-81 for Tasmania against Queensland last week are this season’s best figures by a tweaker. “What I’ve noticed is there have been some great four-day games and some close finishes,” Kuhnemann said. “Every time there’s a subcontinent tour all spinners in Australia have an eye on that.” Kuhnemann appears certain to venture to India, having starred with figures of 5-16 on their last tour to spearhead a nine-wicket third Test triumph. In Sri Lanka last year, he took 16 wickets in the two-match series at an average of 17.18.

Advertisement

As a Test squad member in South Africa, the self-confessed “spin bowling nuffy” watched closely the battles between Lyon and Simon Harmer, as he sought to develop his skill set from a subcontinent specialist to a global wicket-taker. But he believed any chance to succeed Lyon would come upon the 38-year-old’s retirement. “I think what Gaz does really well is wherever he goes in the world, he bowls well. If it’s Australia, subcontinent, he always finds a way, and Harmer does a similar job,” Kuhnemann said. “Nathan Lyon’s the greatest off spinner we’ve ever seen in Australia. I’m just worried about doing my thing and trying to put a performance in for Tasmania.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: 'Reject any implications': Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain
text:
In brief Cricket Australia says it backs Pat Cummins as captain.

The organisation's board voted unanimously to keep him in the position.

Pat Cummins will remain Australia's Test captain despite controversy over his role in the sandpaper scandal.

Cummins' tenure as skipper had been questioned amid conflicting accounts of what he knew about Australia's ball tampering in the 2018 South African series.

Following a board meeting, Cricket Australia (CA) on Saturday confirmed Cummins would stay as captain for the three-Test series against New Zealand starting 9 December in Perth, issuing a statement rejecting any implication that his "integrity has been compromised".

"In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA Board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian cricket and the welfare of all concerned," CA wrote in a statement.

"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The statement revealed that CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met with Cummins in Sydney on Friday.

That followed the announcement that players from the 2018 series would be invited to participate in an independent forum, that would allow them to give their accounts of the incident.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa," Boon said.

"We have learned from that experience, and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins said he backed the forum and intended to participate.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there," the fast bowler said.

"All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins, who has held the captaincy since late November 2021, has steadfastly denied any knowledge of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball in the 2018 series in South Africa.

His stance has been repudiated by Cameron Bancroft, Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers; all teammates of the paceman on the infamous tour eight years ago.

Cummins has described Khawaja's claims the entire touring party knew of scheming to tamper with the ball in South Africa as "nonsense" and has been backed Josh Hazlewood.

Hazelwood said he would have considered quitting if Cummins was made to stand down.

"I think I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," Hazlewood told NewsCorp.

title: The traps, dodgy deals and scams to watch for this Black Friday and Cyber Monday
text:
In brief Many retailers have kicked off sales ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Consumer groups say it's important for shoppers to watch for a range of misleading sales tactics.

One of the biggest retail sales periods of the year is underway. But with it comes the risk of scams, misleading marketing and deals that aren't really deals.

The Australian consumer watchdog says it is monitoring websites, emails and social media for misleading sales advertising.

"Consumers continue to look for the best prices and may delay major purchases until Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of good value and legitimate discounts," Catriona Lowe, deputy chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), said earlier this month.

"Consumers should be able to trust that the advertised savings and discount prices are genuine, but we know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not."

Black Friday and Cyber Monday fall on 27 and 30 November this year, but many retailers have already kicked off their sales.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The ACCC said it is cracking down on misleading sales tactics, including "sitewide" discounts that exclude many products, limited-time offers that continue past their advertised end date, and false claims that stock is running low.

It is also scrutinising discounts advertised against prices that products were never — or have not recently been — sold at.

Here are some of the tactics bargain hunters should watch for.

Deadlines and timers

Setting deadlines is an "age-old trick" designed to rush shoppers into a purchase, according to financial comparison site Canstar.

During Black Friday and Cyber Monday, many sites use countdown timers showing how long shoppers have left to secure a deal.

Businesses are permitted to use these timers, but only if the deadline is genuine.

A number of major retailers were fined following the ACCC's sweep of last year's Black Friday sales advertising.

The ACCC alleged two of the businesses advertised that their sales would end at a certain time, but the discounts continued beyond that deadline.

One retailer offered an even bigger discount in a new sale after the earlier countdown ended, the watchdog said.

Scarcity warnings

Countdowns aren't the only way retailers create a sense of urgency.

Canstar also points to low-stock alerts such as "Hurry! Only two left in your size", virtual waiting rooms to access sales and messages suggesting multiple people are viewing an item.

These messages can make shoppers feel as though they need to act quickly or miss out.

Watch out for fine print

Stores will sometimes advertise deals of "up to 50 per cent off", but only discount a few items to that extent.

The detail clarifying that could be buried in a fine-print disclaimer.

The ACCC says retailers must ensure their sales and discount claims are clear and accurate, and that fine-print qualifications do not conflict with the overall message of the advertisement.

"Retailers should not be relying on fine print disclaimers or exclusions to qualify the headline message of a promotion," Lowe said.

Exaggerated savings

The watchdog will also be cracking down on ads that show misleading markdowns.

For example, if a retailer advertises that the price of a washing machine has been slashed from $500 down to $300, it suggests shoppers are saving $200.

But if the washing machine was recently priced at $400, the real saving compared with that price is only $100.

"Consumers are encouraged to focus on the end price of a product, not on promotional claims," the ACCC said.

"This includes checking for any exclusions or conditions, and comparing prices between retailers and over time where possible. They should carefully consider the advertised price and buy only if the price and time is right for them."

Scams

Buying and selling scams accounted for nearly 59 per cent of Scamwatch reports involving a financial loss in the first nine months of 2026.

These scams involve fraudsters posing as buyers or sellers to steal money, including through fake shopping websites and fraudulent profiles on legitimate platforms.

The government agency says scammers can look like businesses that you know and trust. Shoppers should be wary of social media stores selling products at very low prices, unfamiliar websites, and links received via email.

"Always check the web address, and if you don’t know the store, read reviews, or better yet, walk away," Canstar suggests.

title: Trump's administration is sending mixed signals on chips, China and AI
text:
In brief The US is seeking to combat the spread of Chinese open-weight AI models and restrict access to high-end chips from US companies.

The Chinese embassy in Washington says China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "serve no one's interests".

The United States approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips to Chinese companies over six months, as the Trump administration reportedly considers requiring US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.

The US House of Representatives' foreign affairs committee said on Friday that between December 2025 and May 2026, the US government approved 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD.

All four companies are on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies. The chips sold included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X chips.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the committee's documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips.

Former US president Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Trump gave the green light in December for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to approved companies in China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.

The US commerce department said its approach to H200 licensing "is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial".

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes". The California-based company added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China".

Meanwhile, AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations".

Earlier this week, the US said it would further restrict China's access to high-end chips from US companies, citing national security concerns and saying it would close "dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years".

The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

The announcement came shortly after longtime Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company following reports he had an affair with a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres. The company has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

US intelligence officials have alleged the woman was a Chinese spy, an accusation China has denied.

Before resigning as Nvidia CEO, Huang had lobbied the Trump administration to allow more of his company's chip sales to China, warning that the controls would otherwise boost the Chinese chip industry's competitiveness.

On Friday, California announced it was investigating whether Nvidia misled the public and investors about its chips ending up in China, despite federal export controls.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," US attorney-general Rob Bonta said in a statement.

'Name and shame' campaign

At the same time, the US is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or China, according to Reuters.

The US treasury department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb.

The short-term rental platform uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent.

Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites.

It's unclear whether the idea is gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process.

But its consideration underscores an emerging push by the US to combat the spread of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Open-weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt.

The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI.

Neither the White House, the US treasury department, nor Alibaba have commented on the proposal.

Airbnb said in a statement to Reuters that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected".

The Chinese embassy in Washington said China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests".

"We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests," it said.

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

But some within the US, including officials in Trump's administration, fear China is using such models — like Kimi, DeepSeek, or Qwen — to hook US companies into becoming dependent on Chinese AI.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft through distillation of US models.

Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones to lower the cost of training a powerful new AI tool.

Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by OTSP director Michael Kratsios, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a push by the US state department to highlight such behaviour to foreign counterparts.

title: A decade on from Brexit, EU and UK relations reach a 'turning point'
text:
In brief The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, 10 years after the UK voted to leave the bloc.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and isolated.

The United Kingdom and the European Union have agreed to remove barriers to trade and expand travel opportunities for young people as they pledged to rebuild their strained ties with an "ambitious and dynamic" relationship.

But they left big decisions about softening or reversing Brexit for another day.

In a joint statement on Friday night AEDT after a summit in Brussels, the UK and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap border checks on plant and animal products, cut carbon taxes on some exports by linking their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other's countries for up to three years.

Other areas remain a work in progress, with the two sides giving themselves six months to reach an agreement on the level of university fees for EU students in the UK and vice versa.

The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, a decade after the UK voted to leave the EU and six years after the divorce became final.

Supporters of Brexit argued that leaving the EU's vast free-trade area and web of rules would let the UK take back control of its borders, laws and economy, and strike new trade deals around the world.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and more isolated, and new deals with countries including Australia and Japan have not made up for the economic hit from erecting barriers between the UK and its closest and biggest economic partners.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the deal is "a turning point" in EU-UK relations, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a "historic moment".

"This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe," he said.

This was only the second EU-UK summit since the UK became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from electricity markets to manufacturing rules.

Burnham said the summit was a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.

He said the two sides are "rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago" and "building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market".

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc.

READ MORE UK prime minister says Russia meddled in Brexit vote, pushes for EU return

But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of UK voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

"We remain open to have the closest possible relationship," European Council president António Costa said.

But he also recalled the obligations of EU membership, including single-market principles on the free movement of goods, services, people and capital.

Burnham says closer ties will ease the cost of living

Burnham pitched the package of agreements as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people." He said the deals could bring in £17 billion ($33 billion) a year and add 0.5 per cent to the UK's economic output.

British retailers welcomed the deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products, which will make it cheaper and easier for UK businesses to export to Europe.

"Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow," said Alex Freudmann, managing director of food at Marks and Spencer.

Freudmann said the announcement "is a major step forward".

But nothing in UK-EU relations is ever quick or simple. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in the UK rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the UK has resisted.

An EU official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue. The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.

Talks are also continuing on the UK's desire to be included in the bloc’s "made in Europe" rules, which favor European manufacturers for public projects over rivals from China or elsewhere.

Critics say the deals are a betrayal of Brexit

To get the deals, the UK must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines the UK's independence.

Nigel Farage, leader of the euroskeptic, anti-immigration party Reform UK, told reporters in Brussels that Burnham had taken "the first step, incrementally, to take us back into membership of the European Union".

The war in Ukraine, and the UK's military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and the summit produced pledges of stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the UK rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven UK prime ministers over the last decade and want clarity about the country’s intentions.

Von der Leyen said that a lot has changed in their relations since the Brexit vote, including the pandemic and Russia’s war on Ukraine. She said that the EU is "totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture, the bigger picture" of what ties could look like in the future.

Burnham said he wanted the two sides to do that brainstorming before their next summit, probably a year from now.

For now, Burnham remains bound by the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or friction-less single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the UK

He acknowledged the agreements are "the limit of what we can achieve" before a national election.

title: The controversial export title Australia is on track to earn
text:
In Brief A new report from the International Energy Agency shows Australia set to become the world's biggest coal exporter.

The organisation said uptake in renewables will continue to grow in coming decades.

Australia could become the world's largest exporter of coal within the next decade, according to analysis from an international energy body.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has published its annual World Energy Outlook since 1999, offering multiple views of potential energy futures based on that year's developments.

In this year's report, the agency provided a cautious view based on current policies, another based on policies announced but not yet enacted and a third more ambitious view seeking to reduce emissions alongside alternatives for potential impacts of the conflict in the Middle East.

Since the organisation was established in 1974, energy demand has nearly tripled worldwide. Coal has been the fastest-growing fossil fuel since 2020, with Indonesia and Australia among the top exporters.

By 2035, this would make Australia the largest supplier of coal, with the margin growing further by 2050.

The report described the disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as the "largest threat to energy security in history".

"The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system," Fatih Birol, IEA executive director, said.

"I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

The report said consumers were frequently facing higher prices, as countries' fuel stockpiles depleted.

The IEA suggested renewable energy could rise from 33 per cent of global electricity generation to 50 per cent by 2035 and 66 per cent by 2050. Alongside the growth in renewable energy production, the oil and gas supply shock has accelerated solar, battery and electric vehicle adoption in several countries.

Solar has the largest projected growth, then onshore and offshore wind, hydropower, bioenergy and geothermal.

The IEA said the longer uncertainty persists over the Middle East conflict, the more likely countries will seek to diversify their energy supply and adopt policy to better enable it.

"Countries will pursue different pathways, reflecting their resources, circumstances and priorities," Birol said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) describes a recession as a sustained period of weak or negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP) accompanied by a significant rise in unemployment.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Currently, Australia's GDP is rising, but employment is falling.

Australia's GDP grew to 0.4 per cent in the June 2026 quarter, up from 0.3 per cent in the March quarter — and the national GDP slowed from 2.5 per cent in March to 2.1 per cent in June.

Unemployment hit its highest rate in five years in October, rising to 4.9 per cent – up from 4.1 per cent in January.

There remains no formal economic definition of recession. The RBA refers to a 'technical recession' defined by "two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP".

"Whenever you put technical in front of something, it does kind of give away the fact it's an arbitrary measure that doesn't speak to the reality of what might be going on," Greg Jericho, chief economist at left-wing thinktank The Australia Institute, told SBS News.

However, Jericho warns that Australia's method for defining a recession may be outdated — and thus unable to properly determine one.

Is GDP an appropriate indicator for modern economies?

Jericho said the measure of "two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth" worked well post-World War Two, when there were "manufacturing economies".

He says Australia is now a "service economy" which relies heavily on mining and mining exports.

If an international company exports mined resources from Australia, those exports count towards the nation's GDP figures, Jericho said.

However, the industry doesn't have a high employment rate.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Labour Force Survey from February 2026, 314,500 Australians work directly in the mining industry — 2.1 per cent of the national workforce.

"So, Australia may have exported a lot of iron ore in one quarter, which helped us stay out of recession, but you or I don't necessarily get any money from iron ore," he said.

The artificial intelligence industry is similar.

"The GDP might be fine because we have the AI investment boom, but it's not providing many jobs, no more income, and it's certainly not driving wage growth," Jericho said.

"It might take us out of that technical recession — but who cares?"

Another issue with a GDP-based assessment of recession is that it's "woefully slow" and GDP figures are often revised, Jericho said.

He said data from two quarters isn't confirmed until "six months after the fact".

Jericho said the GDP is "quite divorced from what people are feeling".

"During the global financial crisis, we didn't have two quarters of consecutive GDP growth, but the unemployment rate rose very quickly — over a percentage point in a year," he said.

"People would have felt very much like it was a recession."

He said Australia's Reserve Bank has "consistently" misread the economy this year.

"They were expecting unemployment to hit 4.9 per cent in December next year ... Three months ago, they thought unemployment by now would be just 4.5 per cent," he said.

"It really highlights that their belief that the economy needs to be slowed by more rate rises was completely wrong."

An employment-based definition?

Former US Federal Reserve economist Claudia Sahm coined the Sahm rule, which says a recession starts when the three-month moving average of the national unemployment rate rises by 0.5 percentage points or more above its lowest level over the prior 12 months.

"By her measure, Australia is pretty much right there," Jericho said.

He said that using Sahm's rule is a proactive option.

Jericho said if unemployment is rising by more than half a per cent in a year, it "keeps going up pretty fast and later lines up with GDP going backwards".

He said acting quickly to address unemployment is crucial to reversing recession.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the October labour force data would be the start of an upward trend in unemployment.

"It's probably a sign of things to come," he told Australian Associated Press.

"The number of job losses reported ... reflect the slowdown in the economy on the back of rate hikes, cost-of-living pressures, poor confidence and so on."

Oliver said the rise was a sign the Reserve Bank's five interest rate hikes in 2026 had worked their way through the economy.

But the moves to slow inflation had led to higher unemployment, which in turn boosted the chances of a recession.

"I'd say the risk is high. It's around 40 per cent," he said.

Jericho maintains that Australia hasn't entered a recession yet. But if unemployment reaches 5 per cent, it would be "really hard to argue that we're not".

The Reserve Bank earlier in November revised its unemployment forecast for the jobless rate to reach five per cent by 2028.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said that figure was more likely to be reached early in 2027.

"These numbers, for the time being at least, further downplay the likelihood of another increase in interest rates in December, and arguably also reduce the probability of another rate hike in February," he said.

October inflation data, due to be released on Wednesday, is likely to confirm the next move by the Reserve Bank's board.

Eslake said future unemployment numbers could be a harbinger of a recession.

title: Anthropic's epic $3 trillion debut fails to revive flagging investor confidence in AI
text:
In brief Investors have turned sceptical over concerns about the enormous spending needed to build out the sector.

The Nvidia scandal has softened some of the exuberance for the Anthropic listing.

Anthropic's market value has hit a high of $US2.1 trillion ($3.1 trillion) in its Nasdaq debut, soaring past SpaceX's June launch as investors rushed to buy shares of the world's ‌first publicly traded frontier AI company.

The early exuberance, however, partly faded as the main indexes retreated as the super-sized initial public offering (IPO) had failed to revive faded enthusiasm over AI.

The stock opened at $US111.50, some 34 per cent higher than the IPO price of $US83. But the stock pared its gains and was last trading around $99.

The stellar debut caps a turbulent week for the AI sector, marked by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang's scandal-tinged exit, ‌and shifts Wall Street's spotlight on to Anthropic's rival OpenAI as the industry's next major public listing.

Strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech sell-off offers hope to a sector where euphoria has somewhat cooled in recent weeks.

"I've looked at this ‌whole week as a referendum on AI," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.

"Nvidia gave us a read on the build-out, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies."

From economic growth to doomsday warnings

AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-centre-sceptic Democratic tsunami in the US mid-term elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned sceptical in recent weeks over concerns the enormous spending needed to build out the sector, and mounting debt loads, may not be justified by the eventual returns.

Anthropic, too, has signalled it may tap debt markets.

"At some point in the ‌future we're hoping to ‌be investment grade, and debt is an ⁠instrument that we have available to us, and we'd like to use at some point in the future," chief executive Dario Amodei told CNBC in an interview.

As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $US83 ($123) each, pricing the initial public offering (IPO) above its marketed range of $US70 ($103) to $US78 ($115). Its IPO proceeds could climb to as much as $US93.5 billion ($139 billion) if underwriters fully exercise their option to purchase additional shares.

Trillion-dollar club

Anthropic joins the trillion-dollar club alongside Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.

Although shares can be volatile in the days following a listing, Anthropic's IPO is set to create thousands of paper millionaires and a handful of billionaires,

Based on the IPO price, CEO Amodei and his six co-founders — who together own about 10 per cent of the company — had stakes valued at nearly $US150 billion ($223 billion) combined, according to a calculation based on details in the filing.

More broadly, the listing is expected to create a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, chief executives and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated ‌web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fuelled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.

Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.

"Anthropic is a one-trick pony," Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners, said. "People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won't have that luxury.

"They've got to get to profitability soon."

title: A rising number of Australians want to go off the grid. What’s it like?
text:
In brief More Australians considered going off-grid as power bills and extreme weather pressures grew.

New research found cost savings and energy independence were key drivers of the shift.

As solar and batteries make it possible for homes to make and store their own power, more Australians are wondering whether they need the power grid at all.

Cost pressures and extreme weather are driving interest. Power prices rose five years in a row before easing this July. One in five Australian households is struggling to pay its energy bills.

Queensland is at the pointy end as the state most exposed to extreme weather. Just last week, a supercell storm left 82,000 residents without power. Last year, ex-tropical Cyclone Alfred left around 250,000 Queenslanders in the dark, some for up to ten days.

Fully 25% of householders in Queensland plan to go off-grid at some point, according to the state’s 2026 energy survey, up from 22% a year earlier. Many have already gone off-grid, especially in regional areas where grid connections can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

But we don’t know much about why Queenslanders make this choice. Once off grid, they become invisible to official data records.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In our new research, we interviewed off-grid Queenlanders to find out why people do it – and if it’s worth it.

What do off-grid households look like?

Most off-grid households use solar panels to generate power and a home battery to store it. Some keep a backup generator for long cloudy periods.

We surveyed 40 off-grid households, largely located in south-east Queensland. We interviewed ten householders in depth and spoke to four off-grid installers. We also asked utilities and eight councils what their rules say.

Most respondents lived in rural or rural-residential areas. Their homes largely fell into one of two categories:

• Conventional houses (22 households). To go off-grid, the average house had 6.6 kilowatts of solar panels and a 40 kilowatt-hour battery, mostly put in by professional installers.

• Tiny houses on wheels (ten households). These houses had much smaller off-grid systems, averaging about 3.5 kilowatts of solar and two 4 kWh batteries. Some owners installed these themselves and used a licensed electrician to check.

READ MORE The hidden cost of living in Australia's mining heartland

Why do people do it?

The most common motivation was financial, listed by about 55% of survey respondents. But financial reasons meant different things for people in conventional homes and those in tiny homes.

In conventional houses, going off-grid was mostly about avoiding the big cost of grid connection, which can be $30,000 to $60,000.

As one homeowner told us, off-grid meant:

an opportunity to save some money and work towards being self-reliant.

By contrast, going off grid in a tiny house on wheels was seen as part of choosing to live simply. One resident used second-hand solar panels at about $70 per panel. They told us:

I lived in the suburbs, and you’re just getting bills for this, bills for that. [Now] I can buy some stuff, learn how it works, and kind of provide my own energy.

Other motivations included care for the environment (25%), no grid access (20%), independence and control (12.5%) and finally doubts about grid reliability (10%).

The most common complaint (33% of people) was running short of power during long cloudy or rainy periods. But 20% saw no downsides at all.

Many interviewees described feeling more independent and in control of their own energy supply.

Was it worth it?

Off-grid living makes most sense where the power grid is costly to reach or seen as unreliable. Here, a well designed off-grid system can cost the same as, or less than, a grid connection. It comes with the benefit of producing power for free and keeping the lights (and fridge) on in a blackout.

As one participant said:

"My goal was to be self-sufficient […] generating our own power, sourcing our own water and dealing with our own waste. So in other words, I’m not reliant on any of the government utilities."

One downside was the cost of replacement. Household batteries may need to be replaced every ten to 15 years. As another respondent said:

"The return on investment is 20 years and that battery will probably be dead by then."

Only 20% of our respondents went off-grid out of necessity. Almost all the tiny-house residents we spoke with chose this way of living to suit their environmental values.

Streamlining rules makes sense

Off-grid living isn’t for everyone. For suburban households, research shows it’s usually cheaper to add solar but keep the grid connection. Adding a battery as well can bring most of the benefits of going off-grid, such as lower bills and blackout backup, while keeping the grid as insurance.

Going off-grid makes most sense on rural blocks where connection costs are very high, as well as in disaster-prone areas where long blackouts are possible.

The biggest barrier is whether the rules will allow it. It’s often unclear whether a home can disconnect from electricity, let alone water and sewerage. The answer changes from council to council – and energy companies have their own rules on top.

This situation means many householders are uncertain about what they’re legally allowed to do – especially the residents of tiny houses.

Several told us they were flying under the radar and keeping their home out of sight from the road because they weren’t sure their homes were permitted to be there.

To make it viable for more residents, three changes would help:

Make rules consistent state-wide, with clear pathways for both fixed houses and tiny houses on wheels.

Ensure householders can access independent advice so that solar and battery systems are sized properly.

Collect better data on off-grid households so authorities can plan for their needs.

For a growing number of people in Queensland and around Australia, going off-grid is a real choice. Governments should plan for it in their energy and housing policies.

Cricket Australia chairman David Boon wants the latest Sandpapergate saga put to bed before the first Test in Perth, as his board rallied in solidarity behind Pat Cummins following a turbulent fortnight, throwing its unequivocal support behind him to remain captain. The CA board met several times this week to discuss the fallout from Australia’s infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. On Thursday evening the board agreed that there was no reason to reconsider Cummins’ position despite explosive allegations from Cameron Bancroft that everyone in the team knew of the ball-tampering plot eight years ago. Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood during NSW Blues training in Sydney on Thursday. Kate Geraghty Boon flew to Sydney with CA chief executive Todd Greenberg for a meeting on Friday with Cummins and his manager Neil Maxwell at a “private location”, according to the former Australian batsman, to personally convey the board’s unanimous support and check on the welfare of the under-pressure fast bowler. On Saturday, CA confirmed this masthead’s report that Cummins would remain in charge of Australia’s Test team for the opening match of the summer against New Zealand in Perth on December 9.

“[The CA board] chatted it out for quite a considerable amount of time,” Boon told this masthead. “My belief [is] we need solidarity and we need stability. Pat has without a doubt over the last five years been an outstanding leader and he has been a focal point of a rebuild of the culture in the Australian cricket team. “We saw absolutely no reason to reconsider his role. Every single board member backs his leadership and integrity. Loading “My strong feeling is that there’s a lot of people out there who love the game of cricket and might be a little bit over this [saga]. We know there are things that have got to happen for it to be finally put to bed and we are trying to ensure that occurs over the next short period of time. Hopefully, it settles down right now before the first Test starts in Perth.” Central to that process is the establishment of an independent forum, announced by CA earlier this week, to allow players and staff involved in the 2018 tour to give their accounts of what happened. Further details are expected in the coming days, with several prominent players indicating their willingness to participate.

Cummins confirmed on Saturday, in a statement released by CA, that he would attend the forum and share his recollections of 2018, which differ from accounts given by the likes of Usman Khawaja, David Warner, Bancroft and Chadd Sayers. “I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there,” Cummins said. “All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Loading “Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority. “It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly.”

Boon said the willingness of Cummins, Khawaja and Bancroft to participate was encouraging, but all eyes will be on whether Warner attends. “I think that’s a great show of faith in the process that we’re establishing,” Boon said. “We’re extremely respectful of all opinions and all views. It’s up to us to take responsibility, take ownership, and sort this out as best we possibly can with the interests of Australian cricket at the forefront of mind.” Pat Cummins answered questions for well over an hour. Sam Mooy Boon admitted he had been saddened by the events of the past fortnight and said player welfare was a major consideration behind Friday’s meeting with Cummins, who has had reporters stationed outside his Sydney home. Other members of the 2018 team, including Steve Smith, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, have also found themselves under scrutiny as fresh questions emerge about what happened in South Africa. The bowlers’ accounts differ from Bancroft, Khawaja and Warner.

“They’re all feeling the pressure,” Boon said. “What we think is paramount in anything like this is the welfare of our players – not only Pat – but the rest of the team and expressing the fact that we support them in every way. “Our support for the whole team is unequivocally strong and this includes supporting Steve Smith, Mitch Marsh, all the team members, and the staff.” Asked if Cummins had indicated he wanted to remain Test captain, Boon said: “Yeah, I sensed that. I think Pat is extremely proud to be the Australian captain and he wants to continue to do that. “We want Australian cricket to be what it should be. That’s a national sport for everybody and the pride of the nation. The game needs to unite. It needs to move on together and we need to do everything in our power to make that happen.” The announcement of Australia’s Test squad for the New Zealand series has been delayed amid the controversy – that is expected some time next week after the upcoming round of Sheffield Shield – while some players have been shielded from facing the media as CA attempts to contain the fallout.

Despite the turmoil, and Australia’s 2-1 series defeat in South Africa last month, Boon is confident the team will be ready for the opening Test in Perth. “We’re in a position with the support that’s provided, the talent that we have, that we can move forward and be ready to play by that time,” he said. Loading It comes as Hazlewood broke his silence over the ball-tampering scandal and launched a strong defence of Cummins. Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood rejected suggestions that Australia’s bowling attack knew about the use of sandpaper during the third Test against South Africa, insisting he had no involvement in, or knowledge of, any plan to alter the condition of the ball.

Australian cricket Pat Cummins is under siege. That’s a big chasm,” Hazlewood said. His comments come after Bancroft reignited the controversy through a recent column detailing his recollections of the scandal and questioning the extent of the bowling group’s knowledge.

Hazlewood acknowledged that Australia’s team environment was fractured at the time, with divisions between batsmen and bowlers contributing to a toxic dressing-room culture. But he rejected claims that the entire team was aware of what was happening. “No [I had no knowledge of ball tampering taking place in that series]. We were interviewed straight after [Cape Town] and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after,” Hazlewood said. “It was fresh in my mind at that point. Two things stand out for me from what’s been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? “The answer is no. When it boils down to it, I think those two points are crucial.” The experienced fast bowler also threw his support behind Cummins, praising the Australian captain for transforming the team’s culture following the events of 2018.

“It feels like it’s been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people. I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood said. Related Article Opinion

When pressed on whether he might walk away from the Test team in protest, he conceded it was a scenario he would carefully weigh. “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah,” he said.

Addressing the original allegations, Hazlewood insisted he had no knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper, including suggestions that those discussions took place in the Port Elizabeth dressing room before Bancroft carried out the act. Tea breaks, he said, were generally busy periods for bowlers, who were preparing their equipment and getting back onto the field, often without engaging in conversations among other players. “As bowlers in a tea break. As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before US House politicians on his relationship with Alice Huang. Getty Images This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain”. The tirades were a centrepiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $US5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. ‘You have to do this, or I will rip your f---ing heart out and stomp on it.’ Alleged remark by Jensen Huang “I’d rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,” he once said.

Advertisement

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behaviour kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Related Article Trump's America ‘Vibes have definitely shifted’: The perfect storm that changed how America sees big tech Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear. Huang’s behaviour began long before Nvidia became one of the world’s most valuable companies. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behaviour” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $US1 million, which has not been previously reported. ‘I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!’ Former Nvidia executive Michael Winston on Jensen Huang

Advertisement

Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom US intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, according to six current and former employees, including his own daughter, Madison, who, as his de facto chief of staff, often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Former senior vice president of human resources at Nvidia Michael Winston. He died earlier this year. NYT Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesperson, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behaviour. Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mould of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Huang once belittled Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Harvey Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said last week that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It pained me’

Advertisement

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organisational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the AI boom. President Donald Trump has said reinstating Nvidia’s former chief executive “certainly isn’t a bad idea”. AP Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behaviour was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the HR department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by the Times. In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.

Advertisement

That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Winston said Huang unleashed graphic violent threats. “You have to do this, or I will rip your f---ing heart out and stomp on it,” Huang said at one point. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Lawyer up, Elon. Your astronomical greed and power is about to be exposed Robert Reich Professor “I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston said other attendees were “terrorised” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up”. Winston said he then confronted Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage”. Winston said Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it. Winston said Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Huang told him.

Once every three months, Hayden Flinn sits down to dinner with four other fathers who have all lost a child. He carries a membership to a club he never wished to join – one that has changed his life forever. They speak about youth mental health and of grief and of ways to make the world a better place for the young people of the future. Flinn knows pain, having lost his young teenage daughter suddenly in May 2021 following her battle with mental health. But the Hong Kong-based corporate lawyer says he also knows injustice when he sees it. Hayden Flinn and his wife Dr Sarah Whorlow. Simon Schluter This week, he took the Victorian government to the Supreme Court and won a confidential settlement on the eve of a 10-day trial, claiming he had been unlawfully detained in hotel quarantine for two weeks after his 13-year-old girl died in Melbourne during the coronavirus pandemic.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Courts A father’s rage over daughter’s death has smouldered since lockdown – Brett Sutton is in his sights At the time, in May 2021, there were no local transmissions in Melbourne and the country he was travelling from was not on the government list of virus danger zones. When he landed in Melbourne, Flinn, a co-chief executive of a large Hong Kong law firm, was bussed to a small Richmond hotel room with his teenage son after the pair were refused permission to quarantine at home with family. Flinn filed a lawsuit against the state and its Health Department in 2024, claiming he had been unnecessarily detained for two weeks when he was subjected to indignity and insult, a loss of liberty and mental distress when he was refused an exemption to hotel quarantine on compassionate grounds. At a time when he says he should have been viewing his daughter’s body and helping his wife plan the funeral, he was trapped in hotel quarantine. He argued he should never have been detained, with officials failing to properly assess his personal circumstances, vaccination status and the low risk presented by travellers from Hong Kong.

Advertisement

“It was a difficult time,” he told this masthead. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Hotel quarantine back on trial at worst possible time for Carroll Alex King, partner at King and Collins law firm, estimates the state would have spent in excess of $2 million in taxpayer funds defending its case had the case gone to court. When he met Flinn for the first time, King recalls coming across a meticulously prepared father, who arrived at King’s office with an abundance of material. “The one thing that struck me with Hayden is, sometimes you have a conference with a client and to be frank, you don’t need to prepare that much. Whenever you have a conference with Hayden you have to prepare because you know he’ll be better prepared, and that’s not a good look,” King says.

Advertisement

“That became a feature and ... really just showed me Hayden was completely resolute and driven about this case. “There seemed to be this unquenchable, inexhaustible fire behind all of this which probably came from a number of sources but one of them was … the large expatriate community in Hong Kong, I think about 100,000 people. Hayden would say to me that it had been said to him, ‘if you can’t do this, who can?’.” But what followed, King says, was stonewalling from government departments, including those that manage freedom of information requests. COVID-19 testing at Melbourne’s showgrounds in 2020. Bloomberg “We realised we then had to move fairly quickly because of the three-year limitations period on bringing a tort of false imprisonment. There was a lack of public information, and while Hayden had started digging around, governments are like vaults, they just won’t give stuff away, notwithstanding the FOI [freedom of information] regimes,” King says.

Advertisement

“There was an enormous amount of work done over that ensuing year that when he did a lot of FOI requests to Commonwealth and Victorian agencies, we were continually rebuffed.” King says when the government’s pleadings were finally filed, they revealed the decision by then-chief health officer Brett Sutton to hold Flinn in hotel quarantine had never even been written down. If it were not for Flinn’s discipline and courage and energy to uncover the truth, King says the state might never have settled, pausing to acknowledge it was a massive enterprise to take on the government, with the loser of court proceedings facing the prospect of paying both parties’ legal costs. Passengers disembark from a chartered flight from Uruguay after being evacuated off the coronavirus-stricken Greg Mortimer cruise ship. Getty “In court proceedings for false imprisonment, the usual position is wanting money in damages for that false imprisonment. As part of his settlement with the state, though, Hayden sought no financial compensation. He did not want a dollar for his pocket,” King says.

Advertisement

Related Article Mental health Victoria has the most kids in crisis, but the state government refused a $4.5m funding plea What he wanted, King says, was justice. Flinn is donating every cent received from the government to help young people struggling with mental health. For Flinn’s wife Sarah Whorlow, 2021 is a time she struggles to talk about. Battling to get her husband out of hotel quarantine to be with his grieving family was horrific, she says. She hopes her family can now focus on helping other families in need and spreading awareness of youth mental health. “[I was] needing to deal with coroners and police and funeral homes and cemeteries while he was locked up, that was very challenging,” she says.

Advertisement

“I don’t think Hayden could’ve got through all of this without ... the support ... of friends and lawyers.” Related Article Editorial

Tragedy No excuses. Review of youth mental health services is needed now The Age's View Editorial In a statement signed by Secretary of Health Jenny Atta, seen by this masthead, she says the state regrets the impact that mandatory hotel quarantine had on Flinn’s family, but denies any allegation of wrongdoing. “The state acknowledges that Mr Flinn’s detention caused him and his family significant personal distress and regrets this,” Atta says. “At Mr Flinn’s request, the state has agreed to make a monetary contribution to be used by Mr Flinn for charitable purposes focussing on Victorian youth mental health.”

Advertisement

Hugh de Kretser, the president of the Australian Human Rights Commission, thanked Flinn for bringing his case and ensuring some accountability for the detention decisions that impacted many others in similar circumstances. “Your actions will help to ensure a more compassionate and humane response to future public health emergencies,” de Kretser says. Flinn and Whorlow plan to now take some time to find the right charity for them, one they hope to work with long term and where they can share their own lived experience of youth mental health when the time feels right. They also hope to bring attention to better solutions for helping children in mental health crisis, rather than busy, bright and loud emergency departments like those that their daughter visited before she died.

Advertisement

A close family friend, who asked not to be named, says there remains a generation of young people who lost their social networks during the pandemic and who are finding it difficult to rebuild those. “What is disturbing is the number of suicides that are happening in the community and they’re getting younger. It’s the leading cause of death in people aged 15 to 24 in Australia, and I think it astounds most people,” Flinn says. NRL players believe their season is too long, while their NRLW counterparts feel theirs is too short, according to a survey of almost 1000 players across both competitions. The Rugby League Players’ Association is finalising the results of its annual Player Pulse survey, which provides a snapshot of their views across various topics. Roosters ironman Siua Wong has played more than 30 games in 2026. Getty Images This year there were 969 respondents – 600 from the NRL and 369 from the NRLW – with at least 80 per cent of top contracted players from each club taking part. While the full results are a week away from being released, one of the intriguing early findings was the reaction to the length of the season. The topic is timely, given the NRL only released its draw for 2027 on Friday.

Advertisement

As far as NRL players are concerned, their season is too long; 37 per cent of respondents recorded their satisfaction with the NRL season length 5 or below out of 10. Only 12 per cent of NRL players rated very or extremely high their satisfaction with the season length. As for the NRLW players surveyed, 44 per cent of NRLW players rated their satisfaction with the season length as 5 or below out of 10. The 2026 season was a particularly long one for players who participated in the World Cup. For instance, Tongan forward Siua Wong played two trials, 27 club matches for the premiership-winning Roosters and four internationals, taking his season total to 33. Wong is one of several players who have also played more than 30 games in what is becoming an increasingly demanding schedule, particularly during World Cup years.

While male players have between seven and nine weeks of annual leave, depending on their level of experience, 48 per cent of those surveyed felt pressure to return to training early. That figure is despite the NRL season – from the start of training to the NRL grand final – stretching to 46 weeks. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2027 Every team’s 2027 draw ranked – why the Bears are cheering and rivals left crying “As the NRL and NRLW seasons become more demanding, physically and mentally, and travel commitments are expected to increase in the coming years, especially for the men and women who play rep football, mandatory time off gives players the chance to rest, recover, and spend time with family,” said Penrith playmaker Jack Cogger, who is a member of the RLPA board. “This ensures they’re in the best position to back up year after year and deliver their best for clubs and fans next season.”

A total of 72 per cent of NRLW respondents said they trained and/or travelled during their protected hours (8am-4pm Monday to Friday) to engage in work or study that subsidises their football income or progresses their off-field careers. North Melbourne outlasted a valiant Sydney to book their place in a fourth consecutive grand final, storming to a 32-point victory in front of a roaring crowd at Ikon Park, 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51). A global Ticketmaster outage initially wrought havoc on Saturday’s AFLW preliminary final double-header, with long queues of frustrated footy fans left waiting to get into the stadium midway through the first quarter. The Swans got off to a blistering start, with Cynthia Hamilton booting the game’s opening goal in just 21 seconds – one of the fastest opening goals in AFLW history. Backed by a roaring blue-and-white crowd, the North juggernaut kicked into gear, with Jasmine Garner kick-starting a string of goals. Suddenly, the Swans were in trouble, staring down the barrel of a 36-point deficit in the second term. But, just like in last week’s breathtaking final against Geelong, Swans superstar Chloe Molloy was a telling standout. Molloy kicked her first goal of the game in the second term, becoming the first player in AFLW history to kick 20 goals in a seven-game stretch, breaking the record of 19 set by Aishling Moloney in 2024. Tensions flared in the second quarter after Roos veteran Emma Kearney (a columnist for this masthead) was caught holding the ball, giving away a free kick to Molloy, who converted. When the star Swan celebrated, Keaney ran up to mock celebrate alongside the Sydney crew, with a few jumper grabs and push and shoves included for good measure. It only seemed to inspire Molloy, who kicked her third consecutive goal moments later. After another pivotal goal from Hamilton in the third, the Swans found themselves within 12 points of the Roos and with all the momentum. A soccer-like goal from Blaithin Bogue kept the two-time reigning premiers ahead, but the Swans hit back with a goal in the opening minute of the final term from young star Maddie Quinn. Emma Kearney assesses her options down the ground in North’s clash with Sydney. AFL Photos As the clock ticked down, both sides wrestled for momentum and amped up the pressure. But, seemingly as always, the Roos remained one step ahead, with Garner and Bella Eddey slotting goals to extinguish Sydney’s hopes of a maiden grand final berth.

Swans coach Colin O’Riordan said while the result was a disappointing one for his group, he was proud of their ability to face adversity throughout the season – on-field and off. “[We’re] pretty disappointed, that’s a given,” he said. “You’ve just lost a brilliant final, so yeah, the group is shattered.” Kearney was at her hard-nosed best for the Roos, while league medallist Ash Riddell finished with a game-high 29 touches to go with her seven clearances and 337 metres gained. The Blues take on Melbourne in the second match of the Ikon Park preliminary final double-header. The victors will face the Roos in the grand final on Friday night.

Despite being one of the best players in the competition, the 32-year-old has never won the league’s highest honour, losing out to teammate Riddell last year.

All she would be focusing on is, how does she help the team win next week?” Despite Kim Rennie limping off the field, North Melbourne stressed it was just a cramp.
