The Coalition has vowed to keep VicHealth as a standalone agency if it forms government after next Saturday’s election, rejecting Labor’s plan to wind it up in a move that has won the support of public health leaders. A Wilson government would also seek to shift the focus of the internationally renowned preventative health body away from social causes and onto the state’s most pressing public health challenges, such as obesity and falling vaccination rates. Burnet Institute research scientist Lilian Hor (left) speaks to opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson. Eddie Jim The commitment to keep VicHealth as an independent, statutory authority rather than fold it into the health department was endorsed by the Australian Medical Association, the Public Health Association of Australia, and some of the state’s leading public health advocates. Australia’s most renowned immunologist Sir Gustav Nossal, University of Melbourne professor of public health Rob Moodie and renowned epidemiologist Fiona Stanley on Wednesday wrote personally to Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, thanking the Coalition for its “principled stand in opposing the abolition of VicHealth”.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Bone-headed decision’: Government under pressure to spare VicHealth from axe The three scientists also wrote to Premier Ben Carroll and urged him to reconsider his government’s decision to wind up the 40-year-old institution. “Every serious modern review of health promotion – including work by the OECD and WHO – has concluded that statutory independence and secure long-term funding are the two conditions on which effective prevention most depends,” they wrote. “VicHealth was designed with both features, including its pioneering hypothecated funding model, which deliberately protects prevention spending from short-term fiscal pressures. “Trading a structural protection of that kind for a one-off saving is, on any reasonable long-run costing, a poor bargain for the Victorian budget as much as for public health outcomes.”

Advertisement

The scientists urged Carroll, who since becoming premier has reversed significant policies of his predecessors, to consider the “final, poignant plea” by the late Tim Read, a general practitioner, Greens MP and public health champion, to protect VicHealth. Sir Gustav was the inaugural chair of VicHealth and Professor Moodie previously served as its chief executive. The late Greens MP Tim Read used his last speech in parliament to advocate for VicHealth. Simon Schluter The Carroll government was dismissive of the Coalition commitment to keep VicHealth. “Jess Wilson is going to fund a bunch of bureaucrats and then cut thousands of nurses leaving Victorians worse off,” a Labor Party spokesperon said.

Advertisement

An enduring legacy of the Cain government, the preventative health agency has been in limbo since the end of last year when the government accepted a recommendation by Helen Silver’s review of the public service to wind it up as a standalone entity and absorb its functions into the Department of Health. The Liberal Party opposed the change at the time and pledged to vote against any legislation designed to dismantle VicHealth, which was established and funded through provisions in the state’s tobacco laws. Opposition health spokesperson Georgie Crozier warned that absorbing VicHealth and its ring-fenced $45 million funding into a $30 billion department would see its work disappear into a bureaucratic black hole. In response to questions from The Age last week, a Liberal Party spokesperson made clear that under a Coalition government, VicHealth would remain an independent statutory authority.

Advertisement

“The Liberals and Nationals have committed to retaining VicHealth,” they said. “We recognise the importance of its independence and the valuable role it has played in improving the health and wellbeing of Victorians. Related Article Opinion

Healthcare There’s a simple calculation about health that should outrage anyone who can do arithmetic Chip Le Grand State political editor “VicHealth has a proud history of leading public health campaigns and encouraging healthier lifestyles. We want to see that work continue, particularly as we confront the growing burden of preventable chronic disease. “With an ageing and growing population, and more Victorians living with chronic disease, we can’t afford to treat preventative health as an afterthought.” The Coalition also pledged to retain the local public health units (LPHUs) established at the height of Victoria’s pandemic response. These units, which operate within city and regional hospitals, were an attempt to improve a public health system which, when compared to NSW and Queensland, was under-resourced and too centralised.

Advertisement

The Liberal spokesperson said LPHUs played a “vital role” in dispensing vaccines, providing advice and responding to outbreaks of measles and other communicable disease. A senior Coalition figure said that under a Wilson government, VicHealth would be asked to devote less time and fewer resources to social issues such as violence against women and racism, and more on core public health messaging. AMA Victoria president Simon Judkins and Public Health Association of Australia chief Terry Slevin welcomed the commitment to keep VicHealth quarantined from the broader health bureaucracy. Australian Medical Association Victorian president Simon Judkins during the doctors’ strike in October. Christopher Hopkins Dr Judkins said while the major parties had each made commitments to reduce elective surgery waiting lists and invest more in emergency departments and mental health beds, their respective positions on VicHealth were a “significant point of difference”.

Advertisement

“To be honest, I’m surprised,” Dr Judkins said. “The ALP claim to be supporters of public health but they haven’t come out and made a specific statement on this. Now that the Liberal Party has, they might be rethinking that strategy.” Slevin said Victoria needed to break its cycle of sinking more resources into hospitals and emergency medicine while neglecting public and preventative health measures that stop people from getting sick. “We welcome the strengthening of language by the Liberal National Coalition on ‘retaining VicHealth’ and appreciate the recognition of the importance of its independence and the valuable role it has played in improving the health and wellbeing of Victorians.” Read more on the Victorian election: The latest: See all our coverage of the Victorian election

After Warner’s retirement in 2024, Bancroft’s form did not warrant a recall.

Advertisement

The interesting period is between 2020 and 2024, when Bancroft dominated the Sheffield Shield, when Australia was desperate for regeneration at the top of the order, when Warner was continually failing, and yet Bancroft was not chosen. When he talks about his cricket career being “destroyed”, this is the key period. Cameron Bancroft celebrates a ton for Western Australia in the Sheffield Shield final against Victoria in March 2022. Getty Images Across these seasons, Bancroft was the highest overall Shield run-scorer and easily the highest run-scorer among openers. In the Australian team, Usman Khawaja was enjoying his late-career renaissance as an opener, and his selection was never in question.

Advertisement

At the other end, in these same four years, Warner played 28 matches for Australia, averaged 31.46 and scored two centuries. His highest Test average in any full season was 34.00. The only time he averaged 40 in a Test series was at home against South Africa in 2022-23 when his scores were 0, 3, 200 and 10. Bancroft’s Sheffield Shield statistics over four seasons (2020-2024) 2020-21: 541 runs, 1 century, average 49.18 2021-22: 502 runs, 2 centuries, average 35.85 2022-23: 945 runs, 4 centuries, average 59.06 2023-24: 778 runs, 3 centuries, average 48.62 It looked strange. Were the selectors not watching the Sheffield Shield? Did they have something against Bancroft? George Bailey was a selector for the entire period, with Andrew McDonald replacing Langer in 2021 and Tony Dodemaide coming in that same year to replace Trevor Hohns. Greg Chappell had been a selector earlier in the period, before Warner’s form became a concern.

Advertisement

His dip seemed pressing by 2022, though, when Warner had gone nearly three years and 28 innings with no centuries and four 50s. After his 200 against South Africa in Melbourne that December, he went another year and 16 innings before another ton. His average nosedived. There were widening calls for Warner to be dropped and for Australia to bring in new blood. David Warner had a run of outs but managed to hold his place in the Australian Test team until his retirement. Getty Bancroft seemed to be that option as he was the one piling on Shield runs. It was an intriguing relationship. Bancroft had volunteered to cheat with sandpaper in South Africa when Warner thought he would be under too much scrutiny. He had followed Warner’s instructions on how to cheat. But now, when Bancroft was making century after century for Western Australia, Warner was saying there were no Test-quality openers around.

Advertisement

Throughout this period, Warner’s manager James Erskine repeatedly alluded to Warner knowing more about Sandpapergate than he’d let on. Warner never disputed or shut down Erskine’s veiled threats and Erskine remained his manager. It has now turned out – via Khawaja and Bancroft – that these allusions contained more than a grain of truth. Former Test batsman Cameron Bancroft and ex-opener David Warner have had an intriguing relationship over the years. Getty Images Warner did have dirt on the Australian bowlers. And he had loyalists to dish it out for him. Through 2023, even after he was injured and left the tour to India, after a moderate Ashes series in England (averaging 27.41), Warner was allowed to stay in the team until he decided to retire on his timetable, at the Sydney Test against Pakistan in 2024.

Advertisement

Selectors, with a chronic shortage of Test-fit openers and top-order batters, must still be regretting giving Warner his long period of grace. Or are they? Warner was under no obligation to make way for Bancroft or anyone else in 2022 or 2023. He was entitled to push for everything he got, and he was motivated by his grievance over the heavy punishment he received for the Newlands episode. It wasn’t for him to retire; it was for the selectors to stop picking him. Now the truth is coming out, the question I would like to see pursued is whether the threat posed by Warner’s knowledge of the sandpaper cover-up played any role in the selectors’ decisions to keep on picking him when he was ageing and failing and the batting needed regeneration.

Advertisement

Another perspective Opinion

Ball tampering We need to deal with Sandpapergate before the 150th anniversary Test Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain Were there any communications between anyone at Cricket Australia and the selectors on this issue? Were there any communications between Warner and the selectors about it? Bailey, during his short Test career, had been an admiring minor teammate of Warner’s, and as a selector he chose to frequent the changing room and wear team apparel, almost as if he was still a member. Were there any discussions among the selectors about Warner’s knowledge of the Sandpapergate cover-up, and did they have any impact on selections? Selection discussions are meant to be confidential. But this is an issue directly related to Sandpapergate, and one which Bancroft has raised. It needs to be asked. In time, it may be answered. Bancroft may or may not have had a successful Test career, but he never got a chance because, in a bitter irony, Warner stood in his way.

title: A Wallabies captain was told he’d be back from injury in 10 days. It took two years
text:

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby A Wallabies captain was told he’d be back from injury in 10 days. It took two years Iain Payten November 21, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Twenty-nine months ago, Liam Wright was living his dream. It was the middle of 2024, and the Queensland flanker had not only been recalled to the Wallabies after a long absence, but then-coach Joe Schmidt had also made him the skipper. Wright was just the 98th man to hold the role in 137 years, and an exciting period, including a Lions tour and a home World Cup, lay ahead. Liam Wright posing after being named as Wallabies captain in 2024. Getty Images Wright led the Wallabies to a win over Wales in Sydney but a regulation tackle late in the game saw him injure his right shoulder. The initial diagnosis was he would be back in 10 days. It took two years.

Advertisement

“The hardest part was that it went from the absolute high of captaining your country, and getting back into the Test setup for the first time in four years, to a lot of uncertainty,” Wright said. But now, after enduring an agonising stretch of trial-and-error with an injury that confounded doctors, required four surgeries and many aborted comebacks, and ultimately led to the end of his time at the Reds, Wright is back on the field and loving life again. Wallabies players at the Ospreys (from left): Liam Wright, Marika Koroibete, Lalakai Foketi and Ryan Smith. Iain Payten It has taken a move to the other side of the world, with Wright having recently relaunched his career at the Ospreys club, in Wales. He is one of five Australians at the Swansea-based URC franchise, along with Ryan Smith, and other recent arrivals Marika Koroibete, Lalakai Foketi and Lawson Creighton. There are now so many people speaking with a broad Australian accent at the club, local media has taken to calling it “Ospreylia”.

Advertisement

Wright opened up with travelling Australian media on the turmoil of his journey, his joy at returning and why, despite still harbouring a desire to play for the Wallabies, he would also be open to representing Wales at the World Cup. “The main thing for coming over here was just to really try something different,” Wright said. “I had a difficult end to my time in Australia … so I was looking to just get a fresh opportunity, leave some of that baggage behind me.” Liam Wright winning a lineout for the Wallabies against Wales in 2024. Getty Images The simple version of Wright’s injury was that his shoulder would persistently lock up and lose function. The reason it was happening was puzzling and complex. “It wasn’t clear-cut from the beginning that this is going to be a long layoff,” he said.

Advertisement

“The initial diagnosis was, ‘Oh mate, a little bit of a frozen shoulder, we should have you right in 10 days to play that Georgia Test.’ We genuinely thought, ‘All right, a couple more weeks, we’ll aim for the Springboks Test,’ or ‘We’ll aim for the All Blacks Test’. And then little setback after little setback, it just kind of kept losing motor function. “[Wallabies doctor Gary Mitchell] still reckons it’s the toughest case he’s had to crack, in terms of just there was no real rhyme or reason to why it would or wouldn’t work. Liam Wright, playing for Ospreys, takes the ball in line out playing for his Welsh club last month. Getty Images “I’d get a real innocuous hit and essentially just couldn’t lift my arm off my chest. But structurally, the scans were showing everything is positive.” With varying diagnoses, Wright attempted multiple treatment paths, pushing to be back for the British and Irish Lions tour in 2025.

Advertisement

He returned for the Reds for two games in March that year, but then missed the rest of the season. More surgeries followed. Even for a driven player like Wright, there were many dark days. The 29-year-old didn’t want to retire, but the word did float around him. Wright said the support of his fiancée Sara kept him afloat. “My missus was fantastic. We just made a rule where it’s ‘We don’t quit on a bad day’,” Wright said. “And so it wasn’t an option for me. I knew I could get back to playing good footy, but I understand the way it had to kind of end in Australia as well.” Wright’s contract with the Reds wasn’t extended after 2025, but after surgery on a labral tear and a long-term strengthening program finally worked, he got back in Brisbane club rugby in June 2026, for boyhood club Easts.

Advertisement

Through Ryan Smith, his former Reds teammate who joined the Ospreys in 2025 and has acted as a green-and-gold recruitment officer for all the Aussies who’ve followed, Wright ended up taking an offer to head to Wales, with Sara. He has been outstanding in his five games for the Ospreys, to the point that local media have raised the prospect of him switching allegiances to Wales when a three-year international stand-down would expire in July. Wales coach Steve Tandy has said he would consider it. Wright – who qualifies for Wales via a grandfather born in Pembroke – is open-minded, but a catch-up with the Wallabies in Cardiff on Wednesday appears to have fanned his flame about wearing gold again. Wright and the other Ospreylians have plans to be at Principality Stadium for the Wallabies-Wales clash on Sunday, all wearing gold. “Test footy is what I want to be playing. I imagine myself doing it in a gold jersey and I want to do it for the gold jersey, but I’m not going to turn down opportunities anywhere,” Wright said.

Advertisement

“If the door’s closed for the Wallabies and I’m playing good enough footy to play Test footy and Wales do come knocking, then I’d definitely explore it. Could Liam Wright return to the Wallabies? Getty Images “But I went down to visit some of the boys yesterday, they’re running a real nice tight ship there. “They haven’t quite got the results just yet, but I know what Kissie can do in a short time and I know he puts a lot of care in, so when things start to develop it can happen quickly. “I want to get back playing Test footy. I want to play for the Wallabies, but fate has a weird way of working. We’ve landed in Wales with heritage I’ve now got to explore.

Advertisement

“I was going past Pembroke Dock the other week and stayed there in a nice Airbnb and explored the area a bit, which is where my grandfather’s from, and so things have a funny way of working out.” ‘Test footy is what I want to be playing. I imagine myself doing it in a gold jersey.’ Liam Wright Wright doesn’t have the flashy running game of other Wallabies, but brings immense value as a lineout technician, a leader and a tireless breakdown worker. It is an industrious profile that the Wallabies are short on, as had been exposed on their spring tour. Asked if he was still interested in Wright for the Wallabies, Kiss said: “The big thing for Liam was just getting back into the game.” Related Article Australian rugby Infamous MCG moment won’t drive Tizzano as he faces Lions nemesis in Wales

Advertisement

“I’ve worked closely with him at the Reds for a number of years and he was in that gym, in the physio room, throwing everything to get that shoulder right,” Kiss said. “I just loved the look in his eyes, you know? He looked really happy again getting out there, plying his trade, loving the sense of living in a different environment, all those things. “So we’ll keep an eye on him and Lawson and all the others that are in Europe at the moment. But I was really happy to see him and catch up with him and see how he feels really good about himself again. “And someone of his calibre, we’ll keep an eye on for sure.”

Analysis SportCricketTest cricket Power rankings: The quicks and spinners primed to succeed all-star Test attack Nick Wright November 21, 2026 — 1:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australia’s all-star bowling contingent has achieved greatness, but attention is turning to who will fill their places when they’re gone. The nation will play as many as 16 Tests from December to July, and there is no guarantee the ensemble of Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Scott Boland, Michael Neser and Nathan Lyon will push on beyond the 2027 Ashes. Cummins is the youngest at 33. A home summer against New Zealand will be followed by tours to India and England, a 150th anniversary clash against the Old Enemy, and potentially a World Test Championship final. The ongoing sandpaper saga – from Usman Khawaja’s revelations in his book Sabr to Cameron Bancroft’s explosive column – clouds the future further. The battle to replace the likes of Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins (left) is heated, with Xavier Bartlett and Riley Meredith (right) among the contenders. Getty We break down and rank the men eager to press their claims as the country’s successors.

Advertisement

The quicks: Secret weapon behind next spearhead The prospect of Xavier Bartlett pushing to earn a Baggy Green this summer has taken a nose dive, with his latest injury setback coming after one former international quick lauded him as the man to succeed Australia’s all-conquering veteran spearheads. Despite 19-year-old Mahli Beardman being the man of the hour last week when he claimed 6-21 on his one-day debut for the country, Bartlett was unveiled as the leader of a young attack. While expensive in Australia’s two defeats, his five wickets – trailing only Beardman and Gus Atkinson – came as a wicket-taker in each contest. Loading Before revelations emerged that Bartlett had been withdrawn from the nation’s T20 squad to battle England in five clashes beginning on Saturday night, due to a knee injury, Hamish Bennett – who represented New Zealand 31 times across all three formats, and now serves as the Bulls’ bowling coach – believed he had already announced himself as ready for a Test call-up as early as the forthcoming series against New Zealand.

Advertisement

Next year’s Ashes campaign and England’s swing-friendly conditions are tipped to favour the Queenslander’s strengths if he can turn his purple patch of form – which includes 16 wickets from two Sheffield Shield clashes this summer – into a maiden Test squad selection. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Baby Barrel’: The next Boland leading Australia’s emerging cartel Bartlett will be subject to further assessment before a return timeline is planned. Beardman has also been removed from the T20 international squad due to a low-grade quadriceps train, and is expected to make his comeback during the Big Bash League for the Perth Scorchers. Opportunities for Shield matches have been scarce for Bartlett, who managed just three caps last summer. But Bennett told this masthead before Bartlett joined the ODI camp that a rare period to play in back-to-back contests in October had demonstrated the Gold Coast product was ready to shine with the red ball. “I’m sure he’s one of those names now that [national selector] George Bailey and the likes are talking about, and whether he can be a chance of playing in the New Zealand series or not,” Bennett said.

Advertisement

“He’s come into these two games unrestricted and been able to play a full part in the fixtures, and we saw that when we can call on him at any time he delivers. “He’s showing how skillful he is, and the way he trains and prepares has probably been the most impressive thing about Xav – those little things in how he warms up, how he preps to bowl and how he goes about it. “He’s pretty resilient, he’s had some really good exposure through international white ball cricket and franchise leagues, and that definitely helps develop your craft. You’d have to seriously consider him … his red ball skills are just going to get better and better.” Xavier Bartlett in action for Australia. Getty Images The prospect of an Ashes berth was put to Bartlett ahead of the ODI series against England.

Advertisement

“An Ashes series is a massive opportunity. It’s there, but I don’t want to look too far ahead,” Bartlett said. “If I can put some good performances on the board I’ll be in and around that conversation.” Bartlett said Bennett had been a secret weapon in his rise, and that of Neser ahead of the latter’s breakout 2025-26 summer (15 wickets from three Tests). “A big thing for me [was] trying to keep my ball speed up, trying to stay consistently around the mid-130s for me to try and have a bit more of an effect, especially when the ball stops swinging and seaming, and trying to take some wickets in the middle overs,” Bartlett said.

Advertisement

“Hamish has been awesome. This is his second year with Queensland, and he did some really good stuff with Nes before the Ashes to keep his ball speed up, and we saw the rewards.” The spinners: Frontrunner to succeed Lyon Matthew Kuhnemann admits the thought of returning to India is hard to ignore, but he has rubbished suggestions he will fill Nathan Lyon’s shoes before the “GOAT’s” career is finished. At a time when the future of Australia’s spin bowling has been scrutinised following Lyon being left out of the side three times within 15 months in favour of an all-pace attack, Kuhnemann sensed change was afoot ahead of January’s subcontinent tour. Nathan Lyon and Matthew Kuhnemann. Getty Images

Advertisement

Related Article Test cricket ‘Doesn’t change my focus’: Possible Labuschagne successor thrives in spotlight While the 30-year-old believed some pitches were being tailored towards games going for the full four days, presenting more chances for spinners to shine, his figures of 4-81 for Tasmania against Queensland last week are this season’s best figures by a tweaker. “What I’ve noticed is there have been some great four-day games and some close finishes,” Kuhnemann said. “Every time there’s a subcontinent tour all spinners in Australia have an eye on that.” Kuhnemann appears certain to venture to India, having starred with figures of 5-16 on their last tour to spearhead a nine-wicket third Test triumph. In Sri Lanka last year, he took 16 wickets in the two-match series at an average of 17.18.

Advertisement

As a Test squad member in South Africa, the self-confessed “spin bowling nuffy” watched closely the battles between Lyon and Simon Harmer, as he sought to develop his skill set from a subcontinent specialist to a global wicket-taker. But he believed any chance to succeed Lyon would come upon the 38-year-old’s retirement. “I think what Gaz does really well is wherever he goes in the world, he bowls well. If it’s Australia, subcontinent, he always finds a way, and Harmer does a similar job,” Kuhnemann said. “Nathan Lyon’s the greatest off spinner we’ve ever seen in Australia. I’m just worried about doing my thing and trying to put a performance in for Tasmania.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. A four-bedroom terrace in Paddington sold for $3.31 million on Saturday, $310,000 above the reserve. More than 60 people sought shade in the rear lane of 88 Boundary Street as auctioneer Briannan Davis got bidding underway, taking an opening offer of $2.75 million. After four bids of $50,000, offers then fell back to a series of $10,000 increments so that by the time the hammer fell, 35 bids had been made. Of the 11 registered bidders, eight were active, with bids coming thick and fast at some points.

Advertisement

Such was the interest in the freshly painted property, the initial guide of $2.6 million was revised to $2.9 million based on a late pre-auction offer on Friday. The three-level home had a reserve of $3 million. Buyers were drawn to 88 Boundary Street for the relative spaciousness on such a small footprint of 126.5 square metres. Domain There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The vendors, who were present at the auction, said they decided to proceed based on the number of contract amendments requested. They have lived in the property for 10 years and are moving further east to be closer to their teenage son’s school. The successful bidders were a couple from the inner west who were moving to be closer to family.

Advertisement

Sales agent for Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty, Maclay Longhurst said all the underbidders were similar – young professional couples attracted to the location and the floorplan, which has three bedrooms on the same level. Related Article Luxury property Four of the best homes for sale in Sydney’s east There is a fourth bedroom or home office in the fully appointed attic space, with access via a fixed staircase. The home also has a living and sitting room on the ground floor with the kitchen and dining room leading onto a small courtyard. Davis said the strong turnout and high registrations were due to a combination of factors. “It’s a quality home in a standout location,” she said. “At this time of year when there is not a lot of stock on the market, people have seen a quality home and they’ve tried to secure it.

Advertisement

“No one knows what the new year will hold.” Auctioneer Briannan Davis held the auction in the rear lane of 88 Boundary Street, away from passing traffic, as dozens of bidders and onlookers sought shade on a hot and humid morning. Audrey Richardson The property was one of 666 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Caringbah, a first home buyer paid $640,000 for a two-bedroom, mid-century apartment when they were the only party to register. Although two groups attended the auction of 1/175 Willarong Road, when it became clear that only one was in a position to bid, Mitch Kenyon, sales agent for McGrath Cronulla, disclosed the reserve to them, which was $640,000. The bidder then met the price, and the property sold under auction conditions.

Advertisement

The ground-floor apartment, which comes with a single car space, had a guide of $600,000. The property has been renovated and has an updated bathroom with laundry facilities and is a five-minute walk from Caringbah station as well as the local shopping village. The renovated apartment is 87.3 square metres and has a balcony off the living room. Domain Kenyon said while the second potential bidder was genuinely interested, they were not ready to bid. Related Article Property prices How far property prices will fall – and when they will rebound

Advertisement

“They were hoping it wouldn’t sell and they could make an offer afterwards,” he said. “There are a lot of people sitting on their hands [right now]. “Market sentiment is making people a little bit cautious but there is opportunity out there for people who can get themselves ready,” he said. The vendors have upgraded to an apartment close to the beach at Cronulla. In Russell Lea, a three-bedroom semi just minutes from the popular Bay Run sold for $1,897,500 to a buyer from Drummoyne who once lived on the street. Bidding for 17 Clements Street opened at $1.6 million, followed by four increments of $50,000 before it dropped back to bids of $25,000, $10,000 and $5000. A final bid of $2500 sealed the deal, and the property sold.

Advertisement

Three parties registered to bid, including one who was seeing it for the first time at auction, but only two were active. The property had a guide of $1.75 million and a reserve of $1.88 million. The vendors were siblings who had inherited the property from their mother. The house retains many of its original features but it will need more than a new coat of paint to bring it up to scratch. Domain Joseph Tropiano, sales agent for Stone Real Estate Drummoyne, said while the property did not have off-street parking and needed a renovation, the price point made it an attractive option for entry into the small suburb. “At this level, with the interest rate rises it becomes more manageable [to service the loan],” he said. “It needs quite a bit of work but you can live in it until the time is right.”

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years

Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.
